Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce that the efforts of the government to sell grain to new markets have resulted in one of the largest single sales ever consummated in the commercial field. Agreement with the China Resources Company of Hong Kong has been reached for the sale and shipment to China during the next few months of 40 million bushels of grain. The break-down is as follows: 750,000 long tons of wheat, equivalent to 28 million bushels; 260,000 long tons of barley, representing 12,133,000 bushels.
The grade of wheat will be mostly No. 2 Manitoba northern, which is the predominant grade available in Canada. There will be a limited quantity of No. 3 Manitoba northern. The barley will be No. 1 feed.
The total value of this sale is approximately $60 million. The wheat and barley will be shipped from the Pacific coast ports of Vancouver, New Westminster, Victoria and Prince Rupert.
The Canadian wheat board negotiated the agreement for the Canadian government. The Canadian grain trade, acting as agents of the Canadian wheat board, will be completing delivery and shipment of the individual cargoes, and will undertake the necessary arrangements in connection therewith.
I know that all Canadians will be pleased at the size of the sale. I would like at this time to pay tribute to my predecessor who was in charge of the wheat board before he became Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Churchill). He made the decision for representatives of the Canadian wheat board to go to China in 1958 and again in the fall of 1960. I have carried on with his plans for the expansion of wheat and flour sales to all parts of the world, but I feel that credit should go where credit is due.
The Canadian wheat board, and all others who helped, deserve our appreciation. The government's policy of accelerated wheat sales is illustrated by the fact that Canada's share of the commercial wheat markets of the world has increased from 30 per cent to 35 per cent.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I hope the minister will permit me to interrupt and remind him that the privilege of the floor to make announcements is limited to factual statements. I do so because I have difficulty from time to time with the comment which follows such statements, which I propose to keep within the same narrow bounds. I just feel that in embarking on an explanation of government policy he ought to have that in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, for your advice. I just wanted to keep the record straight.
I am informed that when all commitments are considered the Pacific coast ports will be utilized to full grain capacity until next August, and the heavy movement of western grain during the next few months should have a beneficial result on the Canadian economy generally and more particularly to the workers handling grain, and to the farmers.

Of course all members of the house join with the minister in the satisfaction which undoubtedly must come in the realization of this arrangement with the Chinese mainland, an arrangement which will be of great value to the income position of many farmers in Canada. I am sure the minister will realize that the drop in farm income last year-
Order.

In any event, this announcement will be very well received by the people of Canada.

Sale of Grain to China

The announcement made by the Minister of Agriculture is welcome and important. I trust it is merely a prelude to a continuing expansion of sales of Canadian grain in markets where we have been selling relatively small quantities in recent years. If the minister can do so later on the orders of the day, I should like him to give the house some information as to the price and terms involved, because I think such information is necessary if we are to judge the precise value of this very important transaction.
I express the hope that the minister and the government may raise their sights and attempt to better the target for wheat sales set by the minister at 300 million bushels for the present year. I think it is necessary to get sales above that figure, and if the government is able to conclude further transactions such as the one now concluded I think an improvement in the target should be possible.
This is an announcement of importance. I express the hope that the government will explore the possibility of large sales of wheat to India, where, I suggest, a very large market for Canadian grain is available if the government takes the necessary initiative. In conclusion I would say this is an indication that in an economic sense the government recognizes the existence of the government of China. We suggest that in logic they should now extend this recognition-

Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In view of the interest indicated by hon. members in this subject may I read a letter which I wrote two days ago to Premier Bennett of British Columbia concerning financial arrangements respecting the development of the Columbia river system:
Dear Premier Bennett:
I acknowledge receipt of your letter dated January 13 concerning the subject of financial arrangements for development of the Columbia river.
I was very much surprised that you doubt that the Canadian share of downstream power can be delivered to the Vancouver area at a cost of less than 4 mills. The negotiations between the federal and British Columbia governments have been proceeding for nearly two years, and I am informed that this is the first time that you or the representatives of your government have attacked this estimate.
The treaty with the United States, as you are aware, has now been signed by the Prime Minister of Canada and the President of the United States of America. The negotiations and the signing of the treaty were both carried through with the full knowledge and approval of your government at every stage. The only occasion on which doubt ever arose as to the readiness of British Columbia to carry out the Columbia river treaty as negotiated was on the occasion of the reference made by you last December to the British Columbia energy board of certain questions involving a comparison of engineering and economic aspects of the Columbia and Peace river projects. At the meeting of the policy liaison committee early in January our representatives expressed their concern that this might involve doubt and delay on the part of British Columbia in proceeding with the Columbia river development. Your representatives on the committee assured us that this was not the case, and that on the contrary the reference was designed to hasten the taking of effective action by British Columbia under the proposed treaty. On the basis of these assurances, the treaty negotiations

were concluded and the treaty was signed, as above stated, with the full knowledge and approval of your government.
In the light of these circumstances, for you to write as you now have, expressing doubts as to the feasibility of the Columbia river development "from engineering and financial standpoints", is a most extraordinary development, and must necessarily raise again our doubts as to British Columbia's intentions which we had thought were set at rest by the assurances of the British Columbia members of the policy liaison committee. I do hope that we will not now be met by delaying action on the part of British Columbia.
I am ready and prepared to discuss the financial aspects of the project with you, as we had previously arranged.
I am puzzled, when confronted with the new position which you are taking, which would appear to make our negotiations rather hypothetical, since you now seem to question the economic feasibility of the entire enterprise. I understood that we were aiming to deal with the question of the financing of the project as between the federal and provincial governments on the understanding that both governments accepted the fact that the project is entirely economic. The federal government has no doubt whatever that the project is entirely economic and should be proceeded with and without delay.
We have already submitted to you a generous proposal for federal financial participation in the cost of the undertaking. I shall be pleased to come to Victoria at an early date to discuss these matters on the basis that your government seriously Intends to support the project, and on this basis we can, I am sure, have fruitful talks in regard to the means of achieving the common purpose of the two governments.
I would also suggest that the Canada-British Columbia policy liaison committee might plan to hold its next meeting beginning on the same date as our meeting in order to assist in the early conclusion of all the necessary arrangements for the implementation of the treaty.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house thank the minister for having placed on Hansard the letter which he has addressed to the premier of British Columbia. We hope he will also find it possible to put on Hansard the letter which he has referred to. The tenor and language of the letter indicate that there is not too much harmony in so far as the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia are concerned. As the house knows, a project of this great importance is one where there must of necessity be understanding among the four governments involved. We hope that harmony will be forthcoming in due course.
With respect to more detailed comments on the letter, they will be given to the house at the proper time.

Mr. Speaker, speaking on behalf of this group we appreciate the minister informing the house of this latest letter to Premier Bennett. I must say that this letter and recent
Columbia River Development developments illustrate, in view of past experience, how completely naive the government of Canada has been in its negotiations with the premier of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I take it that the letter was produced for the information of the house and not to introduce a debate on the subject matter of the letter. I hope the hon. member will reserve his comments of an argumentative or debating kind until the matter comes before the house at the appropriate time for that purpose. In the meantime comment is a matter of the recognition of the statement and a reservation of differences, if there are any, rather than an exposition of them.

I accept your admonition, Mr. Speaker, but continue to think what I intended to say.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Finance and ask him whether he will table the letter of the premier of British Columbia to which he referred in the letter which he put on Hansard? I wonder whether that letter could not be put on Hansard in the same manner as his own.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have no objection to the tabling of the letter dated January 13, which I received from Premier Bennett. I should say that I have not asked his permission to table the letter, but I think I am justified in doing so in view of the fact that he gave a statement to the press, I think shortly after writing this letter, as to its contents. I think on that basis I am quite justified in supplying a copy of Premier Bennett's letter to me of January 13 for the information of the house, and in view of the fact that the letter I read today is in reply to this letter from Premier Bennett.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I thank the minister, but I wonder whether we could have it in Hansard alongside the letter he has tabled.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am perfectly in agreement with that, if that will meet the convenience of hon. members.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am not sure that the first letter presented today by the Minister of Finance was to go in Hansard.
It was read.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the house give its consent that the further letter be printed following the letter which has been put on the record?

Agreed.

Columbia River Development [Editor's note: the letter referred to is as follows:]
OFFICE OF THE PREMIER Province of British Columbia
Victoria, January 13, 1961
The Honourable Donald M. Fleming,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Canada.
My dear Mr. Fleming:
Further to our earlier correspondence concerning financial arrangements for development of the Columbia river, and specifically with regard to your letter of December 30, 1960, I regret that it has not been possible as yet for us to meet. I believe, and am sure you agree, that since negotiations leading to a treaty between the governments of Canada and the United States appear now to have progressed to the signing stage, it would be in the best interests of the finance departments of both Canada and British Columbia to discuss the necessary arrangements as quickly as possible.
When it is convenient for you to visit Victoria, I should like to suggest that you would find it advantageous to bring with you technical financial officials who will be able to undertake immediate detailed discussions with British Columbia technical officials on the policy matters referred to them by us.
Like the federal government, British Columbia is anxious that the Columbia development proceed at the earliest possible moment-assuming, of course, that it is proved feasible from engineering and financial standpoints. In that connection, I must tell you that British Columbia entertains serious doubts that power returned from the United States as the Canadian share of downstream benefits can in fact, be delivered to the Vancouver area at the cost of 3.77 mills which has been quoted so often by your colleagues. For that reason, the British Columbia energy board has been asked to investigate this question in association with independent engineering counsel of international repute, and an interim report will be received by March 1.
If the cost of 3.77 mills quoted so frequently by the Honourable E. D. Fulton is, in fact, accurate, then, of course, no difficulty in financing the project should present itself. Until the cost figure is verified through study by the British Columbia energy board, however, the government of British Columbia would of course require the guarantee of the Canadian government that the cost is firm and accurate before it would add its own guarantee to any financial arrangements for the development.
I look forward to meeting you for full and cordial discussion of these arrangements at the earliest possible opportunity.
Yours faithfully,

subsubtopic: REMARKS OF MINISTER TO LABOUR REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext: I certainly do not intend to allow the Prime Minister to lecture me. I should like to ask the Minister of Labour how he reconciles his statement this morning, when he shifted the responsibility for unemployment on to labour and management from the government, with the speeches which he and the government members and particularly the Prime Minister made to the people of Canada during the last election.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: REMARKS OF MINISTER TO LABOUR REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext:
In reply to the memorandum which was presented by the Canadian Labour Congress this morning I set out the measures that have been taken by this government and passed by this parliament in order to deal with the economic situation in the form of legislation; I set out as well the measures that were included in the baby budget. I pointed to these measures as actions by the government to deal with the situation. I also pointed out that it was not possible for the federal government alone to alleviate or bring about a solution to the problem of unemployment, but that it was necessary to have the co-operation of industry and labour doing their part and their share in the production of materials in the manufacturing industry in this country so that it may be competitive in the domestic field and in the export field as well.
Those were my remarks or my pleas to management and labour. I have said these things to management as well on many occasions. I hope they can get together in order to carry on the manufacturing of products
Inquiries of the Ministry in this country so that the whole economy and all Canadians can benefit as a result and more jobs may be provided for people in this country. Any remarks by the hon. member for Essex East in the same form as those he has put forward today are not only a disservice to Canada but a disservice to-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REMARKS OF MINISTER TO LABOUR REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext: That is not what you said in the election.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: REMARKS OF MINISTER TO LABOUR REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext: Order. The Minister of Labour, if I may take the liberty of reminding him of this fact, went beyond the appropriate answer in making the reference he did to the hon. member for Essex East. I feel that he might consider modifying his statement that the hon. member for Essex East, as I understood it, in asking his question was doing a disservice to Canada.

subsubtopic: REMARKS OF MINISTER TO LABOUR REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I correct an answer-

subsubtopic: REMARKS OF MINISTER TO LABOUR REPRESENTATIVES

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: REMARKS OF MINISTER TO LABOUR REPRESENTATIVES

subsubtopic: REMARKS OF MINISTER TO LABOUR REPRESENTATIVES

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, you asked the Minister of Labour to withdraw the words.

subsubtopic: REMARKS OF MINISTER TO LABOUR REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: REMARKS OF MINISTER TO LABOUR REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext: Hon. gentlemen opposite would not let us finish, and we are entitled to point out that fact. As the hon. member for Laurier said, whenever we put a question they shout us down or try to do so. Well, they are not going to shout me down.

subsubtopic: REMARKS OF MINISTER TO LABOUR REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext: I think hon. members will appreciate that this contretemps, which seems to be developing out of all proportion to its importance, will best be disposed of if they will relax and listen to the question of privilege to which the hon. member for Essex East is speaking; and I would ask him to confine his remarks to that matter.

speechtext:

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the right hon. Prime Minister. In view of Prime Minister Macmillan's proposed visit to Washington for talks with President Kennedy, would the Prime Minister consider extending Mr. Macmillan an invitation to visit Ottawa?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: INVITATION TO U.K. PRIME MINISTER TO VISIT OTTAWA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the course that has been followed generally is that whenever the right hon. prime minister of the United Kingdom has visited the president of the United States with a view to having consultations and discussions with him, he has almost invariably visited Canada either before or after the meeting with the president.
I know all Canadians would welcome his doing so on this occasion. I believe it would be helpful if he would visit Canada. In his discussions with the President of the United States he then would be in a position, in discussing international matters, to have the information and knowledge which he will have secured at the prime ministers' conference as to the attitude of the various commonwealth members, without in any way representing them or their viewpoint.
On the other hand, I think it would be beneficial to the prime ministers' conference if it were possible for me to consult with the President of the United States before the conference of commonwealth prime ministers, such consultations to be in an informal manner, to the end that the views of the United States might be available to the members of the commonwealth as we meet together to discuss not only commonwealth but international affairs.
In answer to the hon. gentleman I would say that Mr. Macmillan would be most welcome if he could arrange to call at Ottawa and discuss the matters that he will have considered with the President of the United States generally, and in regard to the international situation.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Port Arthur asked me whether the dominion coal board or my department had played any part in assisting to develop a market for Cape Breton coal in the plants of Ontario hydro.
The dominion coal board have been, and remain, fully aware of all the circumstances connected with this proposed supply. The Ontario hydro officials have been most cooperative and have given the board full information on any points raised.

It is reported in yesterday's Montreal Star that a Vancouver police officer said the night before last that prisoners in the federal penitentiary at New Westminster printed counterfeit identification cards for a country-wide forged cheque ring. Is the minister in a position to comment on that report?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REPORTED PRINTING OF FORGED IDENTIFICATION CARDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not see that particular report but as I informed the house yesterday in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Ottawa West, in which 1 am certain the hon. member himself took a great deal of interest, we discovered in April or May last year that there were certain irregularities in connection with the printing in the penitentiary print shops in Kingston and New Westminster. Steps were taken at that time to deal with those irregularities. I am sure that part of the answer escaped the hon. gentleman's attention.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Has the minister received a letter from Mr. William Mahoney, national director of the united steel workers, in which he has protested that the publication by the dominion bureau of statistics of rate of production statistics for the steel industry has been discontinued as of the beginning of this year? Could the minister say whether he has given consideration to having publication continued?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not seen the letter in question, but the hon. member was good enough yesterday to give me notice of his interest in this matter. Therefore I have had it checked and have here an answer for him.
The dominion bureau of statistics has not discontinued publication of figures on steel furnace capacity in Canada. It has been bureau practice to establish a capacity figure as of January 1 each year, using data supplied by the steel furnace operators. This total figure has been published regularly in both monthly and annual reports. This practice is being continued.
The bureau has merely altered its weekly release on ingot production. This release formerly stated the tonnage produced along with a percentage of rated capacity, the latter being based on a fixed weekly capacity obtained by dividing the annual figure by 52. There were two reasons for this change. First, the weekly percentage figure may in fact be misleading since it is not calculated on the basis of capacity actually in use during the week. That is, it does not take account of forced shutdowns of furnaces for repairs or shutdowns for holidays, etc.
90205-6-105J
Customs Tariff
Second, important technological changes taking place in the industry make capacity figures less meaningful than formerly. The use of oxygen in steel furnaces has increased substantially the tonnage that can be obtained from a furnace. The use of an index based on average weekly output over a representative two-year period appears to provide a much firmer basis of comparison from week to week.

speechtext: The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Rea in the chair.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolved that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the customs tariff and to provide:
1.	That the said act be amended by adding thereto immediately after section 2 thereof the following section:
"2A. (1) For the purposes of this act, goods shall be deemed to be of a "class or kind'' made or produced in Canada if
(a)	in the case of goods other than goods custom-made to specifications, goods of approximately the same class or kind are made or produced in Canada: and
(b)	in the case of goods custom-made to specifications adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time.
(2)	Notwithstanding subsection (1), goods other than goods custom-made to specifications shall he deemed not to be of a class or kind made or produced in Canada unless at least ten per cent of the normal Canadian consumption of goods of the same or approximately the same class or kind are made or produced in Canada.
(3)	The decision of the minister shall be final with respect to the following matters:
(a)	the normal Canadian consumption of the goods described in subsection (2), and
(b)	whether goods are custom-made to specifications. and whether adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time."
2.	That subsections (9) and (10) of section 6 of the said act be repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"(9) For the purposes of this act, notwithstanding section 2A, goods may be deemed to be of a class or kind not made or produced in Canada where similar goods made or produced in Canada are not offered for sale to the ordinary agencies of wholesale or retail distribution or are not offered to all purchasers on equal terms under like conditions, having regard to the custom and usage of trade."
3.	That subsection (4) of section 6A of the said act be repealed.
4.	That any enactment founded upon this resolution shall be deemed to have come into force on the 21st day of December, 1960, and to have applied to all goods mentioned therein imported or taken out of warehouse for consumption on or after that day, and to have applied to goods previously imported for which no entry for consumption was made before that day.

Mr. Chairman, this is one of those rare occasions when I find it possible to take the opportunity to congratulate a cabinet minister. These occasions

Customs Tariff
present themselves so rarely that I never hesitate to seize upon them when they occur.
One of the favourite pastimes in this country today, whether we are dealing with unemployment, exports, imports or any other problem, is to place the complete blame on labour. This is why I congratulate the Minister of Labour for not going along with this very popular trend at the moment. I should like to refer to an article which appeared in Highlights, a publication of the national union of public employees. It is contained in the November 1960 issue. At page 4 we find this:
Union economists who argue that labour costs should not be made the culprit for pricing Canadian goods out of world markets received support from an unexpected ally-federal labour minister Michael Starr.
Mr. Starr suggested in an address to the Toronto board of trade that latest studies in his department indicated industry's profit margin was increasing while labour costs remained about the same percentage of gross value of output.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but is he directing his remarks to the Customs Tariff resolution?
That is so, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I wish the hon. member would point out to the Chair how he relates this to the Customs Tariff. I have been reading the resolution, and up to this moment I cannot reconcile the hon. member's remarks with it.

Mr. Chairman, before I commenced my remarks perhaps I should have explained that this is merely a preliminary leading up to the item before the committee which deals with changes in the Customs Tariff. I presume the resolution has been brought in by the minister in an effort to meet some of the problems of the day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On that point, of course this is one of the methods put forward by the government to meet problems of the day; but, Mr. Chairman, we are dealing with a specific legislative proposal now. It is not in the realm of general debate. I think the point raised by the hon. member for Laurier is well taken, Mr. Chairman. We are discussing a proposed amendment of the Customs Tariff respecting the definition of class or kind.

Mr. Chairman, before make a ruling on the point of order raised by the hon. member for Laurier, I suggest that this matter of tariffs and trade is of vital importance to the country at the present time in trying to deal with the problems before us. I suggest that on the first resolution we should deal with this subject as

thoroughly as we possibly can. Certainly at a later stage I expect the debate will be confined much closer to the individual matters before the committee, but I would suggest that this is the only occasion when we shall be able to deal with this matter as a whole.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. We are not
dealing with the whole Customs Tariff. In this resolution we are just dealing with certain specific things. Perhaps the hon. member has reference to the first item of the estimates of a department during the discussion of which great latitude is given, but this is a specific matter. There is no ruling to make because there is a definite rule, namely standing order 59 (2), which says that the discussion must be relevant to what is before the committee. We just concluded the budget debate.

In that case, Mr. Chairman, I shall have to get right down to the point without painting the picture as I think it should be painted at the present time.
This appears to be just another step in the devious road that the minister is taking at the present time, and the apparent perennial answer of the Conservative party, which is to have higher and higher tariffs. I have seen this coming, Mr. Chairman, ever since September, 1958, at which time the minister brought in regulations and so forth which transferred from parliament to the cabinet the right to set tariffs in this country.
There is one difference at the present time as compared with the old form of Conservative high tariffs. We find that back in the old days R. B. Bennett marched boldly down the road to high tariffs. He came completely out in the open, with no holds barred. Of course the fact still remains-maybe this is the reason for the different method at the present time -that he had his eyes fixed so firmly on that goal, that the result was that he fell into a pit which was 22 years deep. The people of this country were willing to put up with the Liberals for 22 years, following the former Conservative high tariff policy. What we see now is that the current Minister of Finance apparently lacks the honesty of R. B. Bennett. He appears to have the same goal, but he uses devious routes to get there.
I must confess it is a very clever scheme that he has adopted here, Mr. Chairman. This change appears to be designed at the present time to extend the powers of the minister in this field, powers which can be used in a political sense to reward friends and to punish enemies, Mr. Chairman. This is one fact which will bring about fear and confusion across the country, because it will give the minister an opportunity to play off one group against the other. In Mr. Bennett's

days it was at least open and above board, and it was a policy that was equitable to all. It was not a policy that could be played against one particular group at any one particular time.
We need a policy that is fair to all. Whether you agree or disagree with a high tariff policy, at least it applies to all and it can be met with organized resistance by all. What we have at the present time is a policy which puts us in this position. Each group waits, wondering who is going to be next, wondering whose turn it is going to be when the axe next falls.
I do not know what the purpose of the change is, or whether it is going to make very much difference. Apparently aggrieved parties were previously able to appeal to the minister from the board's decision. Now they are going to be able to appeal to the board from the minister's decision. I do not know what the purpose of it is, and I certainly cannot see any difference.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman understands nothing about it.

In spite of the fine words, Mr. Chairman, I would say the result will be something which we have seen coming about in the last three or four years, namely an ever increasing trend toward high tariffs. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this is an even worse answer to our present problems than the popular one I mentioned before, namely to blame labour for all our ills. In the February 1 issue of the Toronto Telegram we find a little article appearing on page 6 which reads in part as follows:
Take the tariff that protects a large part of Canadian secondary industry: In a study prepared for the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, Dr. John H. Young estimated that in 1956 the tariff cost Canadians about $1 billion. It would be more now. This is an indirect subsidy to industry, paid by the consumers of Canada. Ontario, having the largest concentration of industry, is obviously the chief beneficiary.
This, Mr. Chairman, is one of the inevitable results of this trend toward higher tariffs. We have again the warning of Mr. John L. Bonus, general manager of the Canadian association of British manufacturers and agencies. His warning is contained in the Globe and Mail of July 6, 1960 on page 20, and the article reads:
Mr. Bonus warned that it would be a mistake for Canada to retreat behind a production barrier of high tariff quotas. To do so would lead inevitably to further isolation on world trade and increase inability of Canadian firms to compete outside the domestic market.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this inevitable trend toward higher tariffs indicates the government is going back to the old days of Mr. Bennett. High tariffs and economic
Customs Tariff
isolation are going to be for this government an even greater pit than the one into which Mr. Bennett fell in 1935.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rose a while ago when the hon. member rose.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I will recognize the hon. member for Laurier.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
After the statement made by the Minister of Finance yesterday there are a number of questions that come to mind. Before commenting on this resolution I should like to put them to the minister. Some of these questions were asked by my colleague the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and other hon. members on this side of the house. They were pertinent questions with which the minister, I take it, will deal in due course.
The first question that comes to my mind is not as innocent as it appears to be on the surface. It is this. What is the purpose of this section? I have before me the statement which the minister made in the house yesterday. I was in the house when he made the first part of it, but unfortunately I had to leave before the last part was delivered. I note that on page 1636 of yesterday's Hansard the minister is reported as having summarized the three or four points that he suggests are the gravamen of this matter. These points are, to a large extent, legalistic and I think the house should have from the minister a simple statement of the purpose of the section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When the hon. member says "section", does he mean the entire-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I mean the resolution. Then I believe the committee would like to know what goods or commodities will be covered by this resolution. What goods or commodities will be protected? What will be the increase in the rates of duty? It has been said that the rates will be increased from 7 per cent to 22 per cent on items covered by this resolution. I believe that should be confirmed or explained in some manner.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can do that at once if the hon. member wishes. There is no change in any tariff rate involved here. The tariff rates are in the Customs Tariff today. They have been legislated by parliament. This proposed measure does not change a single rate in the whole Customs Tariff.. With respect to those 70 items to which I referred in my opening statement yesterday, there are rates that apply in the case of goods: of a class or kind made in Canada. There are

Customs Tariff
different rates established in the Customs Tariff with respect to goods not of a class or kind made in Canada. This proposed legislation simply concerns itself with the definition of class or kind.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am glad to have that explanation in answer to the question which has been put. However, there are still a number of matters which I feel deserve attention. Why is it necessary to do the things that are being done in the resolution? What industries will be affected by this change? How is this resolution related to the dumping regulations which were enacted by the house in 1958? What effect did the dumping regulations have on the commodities toward which they were directed? Why does the Minister of National Revenue require the powers that are contained in this legislation, and why should he be given these powers which, on the face of them, certainly appear to be arbitrary?
Then why is the right of appeal to the courts taken away, a right which has heretofore existed? What is the value of the commodities to which this resolution is likely to apply? I am sure the officers of the finance department gave consideration to this matter before the preparation of the resolution and are in a position to tell the minister. What is the amount in dollars and cents of goods to which this resolution will apply?
Now, as I understand this and the minister will correct me when he replies if he wishes, this resolution seeks to amend sections 2 and 6 of the Customs Tariff dealing with goods of a class or kind made in Canada. The minister said yesterday the first part of the resolution will be enacted as section 2A of the Customs Tariff, and the latter part as an amendment to subsections 9 and 10 of section
6.	It seems to me that the simplest way in which to put this matter is as follows. When are goods coming into Canada subject to duty? My understanding is that they are subject to duty in two cases. First, they are subject to duty when of a class or kind made in Canada. There is no point in putting a tariff on goods coming into Canada which are not made here. This, I take it, would be in restraint of trade.
Then there is the case in which it is expected that by putting a duty on goods it will encourage a new industry in Canada. However, goods of a class or kind have not always been easy to determine. They have not been easy to define. There is a long history of discussions on this subject in this house. Yesterday in his remarks the minister indicated that these discussions had started in 1904. I have a chronological history which goes away beyond that to 1894, but I am not

going to burden the committee by putting that on Hansard. It is a fact that there have been long discussions in the house over many, many years as to the meaning and interpretation of words of this character, "goods of a class or kind made in Canada," "the cost of production factor" and the "made in Canada" species.
Mr. King, the former prime minister, stated in the house that there were two ways of making a tariff. He put it in this way. First, parliament could fix the rate, in which case it became known to the whole country and would apply at once. Second, the government could take discretionary powers artificially to alter the tariff by order in council, by altering the value for duty, in which event no one would know what tariff would be charged or how long a particular rate of duty would remain in effect. There is a third way, namely the manner in which it is being done in this resolution; because now the minister is to be given arbitrary powers and his decision shall be final. It is of no use for the Minister of Finance to take exception to that statement which was made yesterday in the house, because I intend to repeat it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I take exception to it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Having regard to the language used in the resolution, there is no doubt that is what is meant.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Not at all.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The tariff is a tax. The taxing power belongs peculiarly to the commons, and that power should not be parted with or delegated to any administration whatever.
What is being done in this resolution? The minister defines two kinds of goods, namely goods custom-made to specifications and shelf goods, as they were described by him yesterday. There is no doubt that by this definition he is increasing the range of commodities regarded as made in Canada. Goods that are not classified as made in Canada are not subject to dumping duties. What then is the relationship between this resolution and the anti-dumping duties enecated in 1958? The only relationship between the two is that the dumping law is applicable only to goods of a class or kind made in Canada. This change in the resolution is to broaden the definition and, in broadening the definition, therefore to bring more goods within its purview. It will therefore increase the range of goods that will be classified as made in Canada.
I said earlier that I could put on the record a long list of statements made in the house on this subject. I will not do that but I will refer, as did the minister, to the policy that

was enacted by order in council in 1936. It was that goods would not be subject to duty unless there was Canadian production of those goods up to 10 per cent of the domestic market. The law here is being changed with reference to custom-made goods. In so far as the other kind is concerned, as I understand it, there is no change save and except in the abolishing of the appeal.
In 1958 parliament amended the Customs Act for the purpose of changing the method of valuation. The method of valuing goods for duty purposes was changed so as to include a cost production factor. The relationship between the two is that here they are bringing more goods under the umbrella of this protective resolution. I have heard it stated-and I repeat it because I have heard it stated from authoritative sources-that some $200 million of goods will be affected by this resolution.
I cannot come to any other conclusion but that this is bad and vicious legislation. The minister is moving toward protection furtively unlike Mr. Bennett did. The minister is moving toward a protective tariff in more than one way. He has been moving in that trend for quite a long time now. When he was offered the British free trade proposals at Mont Tremblant, he turned his back upon them and they were not considered. Then we had the tariff increase concerning British woollens. Then we had the quotas on Japanese goods, wherein the Japanese agreed to accept certain quotas affecting exports from that country to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, not at this stage. I would ask the minister to reserve it until later, if he will. Then we had the dumping regulations in 1958. What was the effect of the dumping regulations? I think we are entitled here in the House of Commons now in considering this matter which is not unlike the other one, to a complete statement by the minister as to the effect of these regulations. Why were they not sufficient? Why were they not successful in meeting the ends for which they were put into force and which we fought as strongly as we could in the house?
As a fifth trend toward higher protection we have a redefinition of goods of a class or kind made in Canada. Then there is the question contained in the latter part of section 2A of the resolution which the minister states is not taking arbitrary powers. I should like to put subsection 3 of section 2A of the resolution on the record in order to make my remarks clear. It reads as follows:
Customs Tariff
(3) The decision of the minister shall be final with respect to the following matters:
(a)	the normal Canadian consumption of the goods described in subsection (2), and
(b)	whether goods are custom-made to specifications, and whether adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time.
The minister has been asked first, what is the economic production of such goods and what is the meaning of the words "within a reasonable period of time". When the minister states that these are not arbitrary powers, surely he cannot be serious. The words are quite clear. Here in those two matters, affecting two important items in this resolution, the decision of the Minister of National Revenue is final. Is that not taking away the rights of parliament? Is that not taking from parliament the taxing power to which this House of Commons is entitled?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Not at all.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is giving that power to a minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
It is in restraint of trade. It is restricting trade. It is also in effect, both directly and indirectly, making the capital cost of production higher. How can you raise the productivity of the nation if you are going to raise the capital cost of production? As I say, that is a matter which belongs to this House of Commons and not to the Minister of of National Revenue in any form or shape.
Then again, this section which I have read, in my opinion, gives to the minister new and arbitrary powers, and authority to impose a tax which is the prerogative of parliament. This is protection with a vengeance. This is also protection against something which does not exist at the present time. It is also an invisible tariff. This is obtaining this power not by the front door method, not by the method which Mr. Bennett would have used, but by another method which is being used now by the Minister of Finance, namely the back door method. It is a return in another way to the days of Mr. Bennett, whose policies were so destructive to our economy. It seems to me it has been the policy and the tendency of the Conservative party to resort to these measures in times of unemployment. They may be sincere-I have no doubt they are- in their hope that this will help the economy, but I can assure the minister that in my opinion this is very bad legislation.
There is no appeal from the decision of the minister. There was an appeal, prior to this, to the tariff board, from the tariff board to the exchequer court and from the exchequer court to the Supreme Court of Canada. Now there is to be no appeal from the decision of

Customs Tariff
the minister; the minister's decision is final; he has the full authority to decide these matters, and his decision ends the matter.
I ask the Minister of Finance whether he believes that this is the kind of legislation which will commend itself to the Canadian people. I remember what he thought of powers that were taken away from parliament in days gone by, of powers that were taken away from this house and given not to a minister but to the governor in council.
I remember what he thought in those days, and I would like to put on Hansard a statement dealing with a matter not unlike the one which is under discussion today. To my mind this one under discussion today is far worse, because it is giving the power to an individual rather than to the governor in council. At page 4524 of Hansard of June 7, 1955, the Minister of Finance, who was then the member for Eglinton, had this to say on the subject of certain powers taken away in a matter that was before the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member should say what particular powers and what measures were being considered at that time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It was on the discussion of the Defence Production Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a very different matter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The minister says that is a very different matter, but let us hear what the minister had then to say. I quote his words, as reported in Hansard:
The supreme duty of parliament, in discharging its responsibility to the people, is to be true and faithful to its traditional role of the champion of the rights and freedom of the people.
Then he said:
How this government loves to dress up what is in fact a denial of the rule of law, the subjugation of parliament to the executive branch of government, by having parliament go through the process of conferring upon them the power to legislate. And that vicious practice is dressed up. An attempt is made to clothe it with an air of respectability by calling it ''delegated legislation". Sir, no euphonious title will succeed in applying a sufficient disguise to this vicious and threatening practice.
Hon. members can well see, in the light of the description of the Prime Minister of the powers under this act, that these are such powers as make it possible for the government to make itself dictator of the Canadian economy tomorrow. Under this legislation the government, and particularly the Minister of Defence Production, hold the Canadian economy in the palms of their hands. The government can override any other legal obligation howsoever created.
Sir, these powers are so sweeping that I am quite sure most Canadians just could not believe this is the way in which parliament is called upon by this government to legislate.

Those are the words of the Minister of Finance of yesteryear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And very true they were, in the circumstances.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Those words are applicable to this legislation.
They are much more so.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They are much more true in this case, as my hon. friend the member for Bonavista-Twillingate says, when the powers will be conferred not upon the executive but upon the Minister of National Revenue, as contained in the second part of this resolution.
And without appeal.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
And without appeal. This is really dressing it up. Where could you dress it up any more than you have in the resolution and as you probably will in the bill?
I said earlier that this, in my opinion, was vicious legislation. The Minister of Finance and some of his colleagues have gone to Paris, to Washington and elsewhere in an attempt to come to some understanding with the common market countries. The common market countries up until now, as I understand it, have reduced their tariffs by some 30 per cent and are prepared to raise their tariffs against countries on the outside. Canada, the United States and Britain may well be affected by this unless Britain joins the common market, and unless Canada and the United States give greater consideration to a modus vivendi between the two blocs, because there is no doubt in the world that the economy of the common market is in high gear at the present time.
This is the kind of legislation which in my opinion is giving effect to the threat which the Minister of Trade and Commerce expressed in a speech delivered in Paris, and which the Leader of the Opposition has already put on Hansard. In view of that it would seem to me that attempts should be made to find a common denominator between the economy of those countries and that of Canada, Britain and the United States, rather than resorting to this kind of legislation, which undoubtedly will have a detrimental effect on our country.
I repeat what 1 said earlier. I do not think this legislation will meet the position which the minister has in mind, and I can only repeat what he said:
Sir, these powers are so sweeping that I am quite sure most Canadians just could not believe this is the way in which parliament is called upon by this government to legislate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Laurier began by indicating that he had not heard half of the statement

that I made yesterday by way of explanation of the resolution. I can well understand that, after having listened to his remarks this afternoon, because they have not been directed to the resolution at all. He may have thought he was speaking about the resolution, but he was talking about something quite different from what is before the house.
He began also by saying he was going to ask a series of questions, and I gathered the impression that he was going to wait for the answers before he launched into any statement of his position on the bill. But he has not waited to obtain the information in reply to some eight or ten questions. He went on, not waiting for the information, not waiting for the answers; indeed, not caring to wait until he received information that evidently he was aware of needing. He then proceeded to attack the bill and to denounce it with adjectives which can only be construed as indicating that he is not aware of the terms of the legislation proposed.
I am going to begin by offering him the kind of information that I thought he was seeking, and suggest that had he had this information he would have come to a rather different conclusion. I also have some observations to make on some other long bows that he has drawn on the record of this government in relation to matters pertaining to tariff protection.
His first question was, "What is the purpose of this resolution?" I stated that in the budget speech of December 20, and I stated it again yesterday. It is very clear. The purpose of the proposed legislation is to restore the original concepts relating to this phrase "class or kind" after what I described yesterday as a decade of erosion. In doing so we will provide for the first time some effective means of dealing with goods that have been described in this proposed amendment.
The second of his questions was, "What goods or commodities are covered by the resolution?" I have already answered that. They are all set out in the Customs Tariff in the 70 items in which this expression appears. They cover a very broad range of goods. In most cases there is no question about whether goods are made or not made in Canada, but difficulties have arisen over marginal cases. These have always been subject to the rulings of the department. The hon. member knows perfectly well that this legislation, which has been on the statute books for many years, has required rulings to be made times without number by the department.
Which were appealable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, they were subject to appeal. I am dealing now with the situation as regards the interpretation of 90205-6-106
Customs Tariff
legislation the meaning of which was well understood, especially by the governments which introduced it, principally Liberal governments, and I say that the course of the decisions in the past decade has been to set at nought in many of these cases the purpose of parliament and the purpose of the governments which introduce this legislation.
Would the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was denied the privilege of asking the hon. member for Laurier a question, but I do not wish to follow his example.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You interrupted me and made a speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not do anything of the kind. I asked if I could ask a question, and the hon. gentleman said no.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Just a moment. I will not allow the Minister of Finance to misinterpret what happened. The hon. gentleman interrupted me in the early part of my speech and proceeded to make a statement. I did not deny him that opportunity. Then he asked if he could ask a question and I denied him the right to ask that question because I did not want my speech to be interrupted by a number of statements from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I come back to what I said. The hon. member is referring to the question he asked me, his second question. I indicated I was prepared to answer that at that time. He yielded the floor, and I then answered his second question. Later, when the hon. gentleman reached the point of talking about export quotas applied by Japan on certain exports to Canada, I rose and asked, in accordance with the rules of the house, if I could ask a question then, and the hon. gentleman said, no. The record will bear me out.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You interrupted me then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, there was no interruption at all; none whatever.
I will deal with the question asked by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

Does the minister mean by what he is pleased to call "erosion" the decisions of the courts and, if so, is he not asking this parliament to overrule and override the courts because he does not like their decisions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is a fact that that there have been decisions of the courts in this period, decisions which have been at variance with the rulings and interpretations which had been well established up to that time.

Customs Tariff
The rulings of the executive.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of Liberal governments, principally-
Still the executive.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -of which the hon. gentleman's colleagues were previously members.
That does not alter the principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This parliament changes the law very often in the light of the interpretation of the law by the courts.
May I ask the minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Legislation by parliament-
May I ask the minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I finish my statement?
I beg the minister's pardon.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Many of the proposals put before parliament in the course of budgets arise out of interpretations which the courts have placed on certain measures. There is hardly a budget placed before parliament which does not take note in some respect or other of an interpretation put on something by the courts and the necessity for changing the law as thus interpreted by the courts. Let there be no mistake about that. In recent years, as a result of one or two of the decisions which the tariff board has been following, interpretations have been given by the courts which, again, have carried an emphasis which is at variance with what was the well-established import of those words prior to this last decade. That is an uncontestable fact.

May I ask the minister if he will now answer my question. I accept what he has said that parliament has a perfect right to change laws after the courts have made decisions. If the courts place a certain interpretation on the law and we think it should be something else, then we have the right to change it, but what the minister is asking here is that we should suppress the courts. He is denying the right to an appeal in the future, and that is what we are objecting to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You see, Mr. Chairman, this speech has been introduced under the guise of asking a question.
Well, answer it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Answer the speech? I shall be prepared to answer anything that is raised in the committee and I shall be

prepared to answer this point, but I will first draw to your attention, Mr. Chairman, the manner in which the hon. member, having taken to himself the right to ask a question, then comes forward in typical style to supply his own answer, which is a most erroneous and misleading answer, and then sits down with a look of utter satisfaction although the answer he has supplied to his own question is wrong.
You give the answer, then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I make my own statement?
Give the answer; never mind all the verbiage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We were referring a moment ago to interruptions. You will note, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member is still not satisfied. He has asked a question and supplied his own answer and now when I am dealing with the subject he insists that he should supply my answer as well. The process of totalitarianism with which the hon. member is all too well acquainted has not gone that far here. The hon. gentleman is not going to supply the answer for me.
I had reached the point, before the hon. member's interruption, where I was dealing with the second question put by the hon. member for Laurier. Quite at variance with his idea of the effect of this amendment I say that there are no rates changed by this legislation. This legislation does not change a single customs tariff rate under the Customs Tariff.
We are asked, in the third place, what industries are affected. They are the industries which are engaged in the production of the articles described in these 70 items in the Customs Tariff. They cover a wide range but, as I indicated, if you are looking in particular at one branch of the goods, namely those described here as custom-made according to specification, they are obviously heavy machinery in large measure.
I was asked next by the hon. member for Laurier how this is related to the dumping regulations. The form of the question is very interesting. What does the hon. gentleman mean by "dumping regulations"? The dumping regulations which I presume he has in mind must be some regulations promulgated in pursuance of legislation passed by parliament. He is quite right in saying that the powers which are created under the Customs 1 ariff in relation to dumping apply only to goods of a class or kind made in Canada. That is quite correct and I dealt with that subject in my remarks yesterday. I pointed that out plainly. Then when he went on to talk about this subject later it appeared that

when he talked about dumping regulations he had some reference to the legislation which was introduced in 1958 in this house by way of amendment to the Customs Act. That is not this statute at all; it is the Customs Act. That was a measure introduced by a colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, dealing with the basis of valuation of goods imported into Canada and requiring that certain elements of cost of production be included in that value for entry purposes.
At a later stage in his speech, without having waited for an answer to this question, we heard the hon. member say that the present legislation apparently had some sinister connection with the legislation of 1958. The legislation of 1958 was very good legislation and as was pointed out at that time it was badly needed for the purpose of making known to some foreign producers who were in the habit of exporting into Canada that they would not be permitted to do so on a basis of dumping in Canada.
So salutary has been the effect of the mere enactment of that legislation that it has not been necessary once in the two and a half intervening years to apply that legislation in any particular case. The Minister of National Revenue made that fact known in the house previously. I say there is an exemple of very great benefit having been achieved by the mere enactment of that legislation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All this talk about arbitrary powers has no application whatever. It never had any basis and it has none now.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, contrary to the position taken by the hon. member when he was speaking, I shall be glad to answer his question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I thank the hon. minister, Mr. Chairman, but I should like to ask him this question. How salutary could the regulations to which he referred have been when in the constituency of Stormont and in the city of Cornwall no less than two industries closed down?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I draw attention to the evidence of a continued and sad misconception on the part of the hon. member for Laurier. I have been talking about legislation, amendments to the Customs Act enacted in this house in the 1958 session. The hon. member comes back and talks about the dumping regulations. 1 am left to wonder what the hon. member is talking 90205-6-106i
Customs Tariff
about or whether he clearly understands what the matter is that is now before the committee.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The two thousand people who are out of work are wondering too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member apparently is saying that more drastic use should have been made of the powers conferred by parliament upon the Minister of National Revenue.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The minister is saying that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Otherwise the hon. member's statement has no sense in it whatever.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The minister is saying that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Here we are getting interruptions, you see, from the hon. member who was complaining about interruptions when he did not get any. Perhaps the hon. gentleman can listen now when someone else has the floor.
The fact is, Mr. Chairman, that this was salutary legislation. It has had a good effect. The hon. member for Laurier having opposed that legislation in 1958 is now saying ii* effect, "You should exercise powers now that I objected to your taking in 1958." This is just about as consistent as one might expect in that particular quarter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Two thousand people out of work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There he goes again, Mr. Chairman, and yet the hon. member was complaining about interruptions.
I now proceed to the hon. member's next question which was this: Why does the minister require the powers? I dealt with this subject yesterday and I will come back again to this subject of the powers of the minister and of the tariff board in relation to the matters that are going to arise under the proposed amendment. I again draw the attention of the committee to the fact that the hon. member is apparently not aware that the legislation as it has existed in its present form for years has required many decisions on the part of the minister. But I will come back to this matter of the powers of the minister and of the tariff board in relation to the amendments because there has been, not only a sad misinterpretation but indeed a drastic misrepresentation of the effect of the amendments in that regard.
Lack of clarity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In question No. 6 the hon. member asks why the right of appeal is taken away. I say that the right of appeal as to matters that are properly the subject

Customs Tariff
of appeal is not taken away by this legislation. Again I shall have something to say by way of enlargement on this matter at a later stage in my remarks.
In his next question the hon. member asks what is the value of the commodities to which the resolution is likely to apply. The fact is that no one can say precisely what is the value of the commodities to which the amendment is likely to apply. This case is not at all the simple case in which there is a change in the rate of duty on an existing tariff item. In such cases statistics are usually available including the volume of imports which would be affected. In the present situation, however, what is involved is some alteration in the position of the margin between what is considered to be made in Canada and what is not.
There are two reasons why statistics cannot be given here in reply to this question. In the first place, in the case of many pairs of tariff items-and when I speak about pairs I am speaking about items including those that are made in Canada on the one hand and those that are not made in Canada on the other; that is what is meant by a pair-statistics exist only for total imports. In the second place it is not possible to forecast what quantitative effects will flow from rulings based on the new section as opposed to rulings based on the former section.
The hon. member's next question, I think, was really the same question re-phrased. He asked what was the amount in dollars and cents of such commodities. I have dealt with that.
The hon. member next asked when are goods coming into Canada subject to duty. The answer is that they are subject to duty when the Customs Tariff makes them subject to duty. That is legislation with which we are not interfering in the least. I say again that this legislation does not change any rate whatever. Broadly speaking the rates are lower in the case of goods not produced in Canada under these 70 items of the tariff than are the rates on goods that are produced in Canada.
I wish now to proceed to deal more broadly with some of the remarks of the hon. member for Laurier and hon. members who preceded him. The hon. gentleman spoke about the history of this legislation. He is aware of history going back to 1894. Actually, if you wish to go to the fine point, this kind of legislation goes back to 1873 for it was in that year that provision was made for a 10 per cent duty on "machinery for mills and factories of kinds which are then 
manufactured in the dominion." There was further legislation in 1880 and again in 1890, and so on.
My reference to this legislation yesterday as coming from 1907 related largely to the form of the present tariff. It is in that tariff that we find this present concept appearing and carried to a greater extent than had ever been done before in any legislation of this parliament.
We have had statements made to the effect that this proposed legislation gives the government or the minister power which, as the hon. member for Laurier said, belongs to the house. The hon. gentleman said that Mr. King had once stated that there were several ways of applying tariffs and one way was to take unto the governor in council the power to establish the tariff by order in council.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member said that Mr. King had said that this was one of several ways in which a tariff could be established. I have his words here. The hon. gentleman said in effect that the better way was to legislate directly and not to give the governor in council power to establish rates by order in council. It is unfortunate that the hon. member for Laurier was not better prepared with his case before he began to talk along this line today. We are asking the house in these present amendments to reduce the powers that the Customs Tariff now confers on the governor in council.
Subject to appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, the powers to which I am referring are not subject to appeal at all.
Do not become angry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I sometimes find it difficult to be completely patient and docile in the face of statements emanating from hon. members opposite that are not only erroneous but misleading.
Docility is not one of your qualities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not hear the remark, but I take it that it comes from a source that probably one should not take the time to deal with, anyway.
That is because it is injurious to you.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The source in question I should think is injurious to everything, including itself.

The hon. member waxed quite loud on this subject. He evidently does not like powers being given to the governor in council. Well, Mr. Chairman, let me draw his attention to powers that parliament has given to the governor in council, which we are in effect now giving back to parliament if parliament will approve the present resolution. Under section 6, subsection 10, of the present Customs Tariff we have this provision:
For the purpose of this act goods shall not be deemed to be of a class or kind made or produced in Canada unless so made or produced in substantial quantities, and-
And note these words, Mr. Chairman:
-the governor in council may provide that such quantities, to be substantial, shall be sufficient to supply a certain percentage of the normal Canadian consumption and may fix such percentages.
This is the section, Mr. Chairman, and it is under the authority of this clause that the Liberal government in 1936 proceeded to pass order in council P.C. 1618 on July 2, 1936, and to name as 10 per cent the percentage of the normal Canadian consumption which an article must supply before it is to be deemed to be a class or kind made in Canada.
Will the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I just go on. I will be glad to take the question at the proper time, but I am in the middle of developing a point here.
This is the order in council passed by the Liberal administration. It is significant that it was passed in 1936, in the first or the second session that the hon. member for Laurier was a member of this parliament. I have no doubt that since this legislation was introduced by the government of that day it had his full support.
The legislation was not introduced then; it was the order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The order in council was introduced at that time, and I have no doubt that since it was introduced by the government of that day it must have had the full support of the hon. member for Laurier. I do not recall that he has ever raised his voice in protest against the exercise of this power.
Now, Mr. Chairman, as long as this power remains on the statute books it lies within the power of the governor in council to change that percentage requirement. It will be perfectly lawful for the governor in council to pass a new order in council and say that the order in council of 1936 is repealed and that hereafter articles shall not be deemed to be a class or kind made or produced in Canada unless a quantity sufficient to supply 1 per cent-
Customs Tariff
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -of the normal Canadian consumption of such article was made or produced. That is the power, and that would be a perfectly valid exercise of this power that parliament has conferred on the governor in council, and that is the sort of exercise of such a power that I would expect to be carried out by a government that had a high tariff or a high protection purpose. It would be the easiest thing in the world, and the hon. member has the temerity to accuse the present government of having a high protection purpose in what it is doing.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is no doubt about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The facts are all against the hon. member for Laurier.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are. In the teeth of the argument that he put before the committee this afternoon is the answer that we are not using the power that we could use to reduce to some vanishing point, some merely nominal percentage, the requirement in order that the higher tariff rate should become applicable, because the goods would then be classed as a class or kind made in Canada.
