We are, on the contrary, taking this power away from the governor in council and we are asking parliament to legislate. We are doing the very thing that the hon. member for Laurier-if he understood the full significance of the words he used this afternoon, or probably he was ascribing them to Mr. Mackenzie King-says that he would have been doing. He should be supporting our amendment instead of purporting to say, as he did, that we were violating, as I understood him, those principles on which he was taking a stand. He says that this is bad, vicious legislation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hope he will go down to Cornwall and say to the people there that he is against anything in the way of protection; that he has stood up in this House of Commons and denounced what he said was a protective measure, even though the facts seem to be somewhat different.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The minister should go down to Cornwall and explain his stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Here is a member who has asked me repeatedly in the house about what measures we are taking to prevent goods coming into Canada to displace those made by the textile mills in Cornwall. I hope that the workmen in the textile mills in Cornwall will be well informed of this; I hope

Customs Tariff
that they will know that their former member for Cornwall has risen in his place today and has attacked legislation that he said had a protective purpose because it had such a purpose, in his assertion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I rise on a point of order and a question of privilege. The Minister of Finance has no right to make statements such as those he has made, and he has no right to insinuate. He has asked questions in connection with a question which I put to him, and from what was said has drawn a conclusion. I did not deal in my remarks with anything concerning the textile industry or with anything concerning the mills in Cornwall. In his reply to me my hon. friend knows-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: What is the point of order?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The point of order is that I have been misrepresented by the Minister of Finance. I have been misrepresented not only in the words which he used but also in the interpretation which he put on my remarks. At no time in the remarks which I made did I refer to the textile mills in Cornwall. When a question was put to me I did ask, what was being done by the anti-dumping regulations in so far as the 2,000 people put out of work in the mills at Cornwall are concerned. I will meet my hon. friend on that point here in the house at any time he wishes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: What is the point of order?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The point of order is that the anti-dumping regulations were enacted in this house with the stated view of coming to the assistance of those who were in difficulties and those who suffered in those mills. So far as I can see not a thing has been done to assist them in any way whatsoever. When the minister makes a statement he should not attempt to put words in an hon. member's mouth which were not there at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is the phoniest point of order ever raised in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I quite agree with my hon. friend from Carleton that what we have just heard is just about the phoniest point of order that has been raised in this house. The hon. member obviously wished to make his speech. He is not content to wait and do so in the proper way, so he raises a bogus point of order. Let us not worry about that, Mr. Chairman. We have this interesting situation. The hon. member for Laurier was one of those who believed that the workers in the textile mills in Cornwall should have some protection against dumping in the Canadian market of the kind of goods that they were seeking to make in the Cornwall mills.

The hon. member apparently has not realized yet that the power to deal with dumping is confined to goods of a class or kind made in Canada, and the erosion that has gone on over the past 10 years has gradually narrowed the power reposed in the government by parliament to deal with the dumping of goods of another nature that are of a class or kind made in Canada, and that applies to the textile goods made in those Cornwall mills.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You put 2,000 out of work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Everything said by the hon. member for Laurier, everything that has been argued for this afternoon, confounds him when he pretends to be a champion of the workers in the textile mills. He has argued here this afternoon for a position that would gradually reduce the power of government to apply dumping measures to restrain the kind of dumping that would otherwise deprive Canadians of their jobs in those textile mills in Cornwall.
Now, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate, in seeking to come to the rescue of the hon. member for Laurier, was a little too quick on the trigger a moment or two ago, as he so often is. I should like to caution my old friend, the hon. member for Laurier, against accepting gratuitous aid from that uncertain quarter. I think that his own mistakes in his speech this afternoon were such that he would be better advised to stick with those than to accept the Trojan horse offered by his seatmate, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
The order in council to which I have referred, Mr. Chairman, P.C. 1618 of July 2, 1936, was passed under the authority of subsection 10 section 6 of the Customs Tariff, as I have indicated. I did not go on to state, as I should have at that time, that that subsection, which gives to the governor in council the power to determine the percentage which shall be the test whether goods are of a class or kind made in Canada, was itself enacted in this house in 1936. It was part of the budget proposals introduced by the Liberal minister of finance in 1936, and was supported by the hon. member for Laurier. It was after that subsection was enacted by parliament that the power thereby conferred on the governor in council was exercised in the manner I have indicated.
Now, I proceed to another interesting observation made by the hon. member for Laurier.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; I am sorry to interrupt the minister but his time has expired.

I can give the minister a chance to continue by saying about five words because I think we would like him to continue. I wonder if the minister would not go

on and answer the question I asked, and on which he beat around the bush and carefully evaded an answer. My question is this: Why is the government, instead of changing the law and undoing this so-called erosion but still leaving the right of appeal to the courts, abolishing the appeal to the courts by this legislation? Subsection 3 of section 2A of the proposed resolution reads:
The decision of the minister shall be final with respect to the final matters:
(a) the normal Canadian consumption of the goods described in subsection 2,-
If the minister's decision about that is final, the minister can set that at any figure he chooses. No matter what other aspects of the matter may be appealed to the courts, if the minister says normal consumption is only 100 of something, then 10 per cent would only be 10. If you give this control and completely arbitrary power to the minister then there is nothing whatever left for determination on the appeal. I ask the minister why, when he attaches great virtue to this government for putting the 10 per cent into the law instead of leaving it in the regulations, he changes the definition of class or kind to make it uncertain when formerly it was precise and certain. I believe that the change with respect to the 10 per cent, of itself and isolated from everything, is commendable. However, this resolution gives to a single minister the arbitrary power, without appeal, to determine the quantity that is normally consumed in Canada.
The moment you abstract one element from the adjudication, no adjudication can be made at all. Unless the tariff board has the power to decide the quantity normally consumed in Canada it cannot make any proper decision as to what 10 per cent of that is. This decision will be governed by the amount the minister may arbitrarily determine. If the minister has some friends who want some protection he can set the total quantity very low in order to make sure their production is 10 per cent, thus giving them a hand-out. If, on the other hand, there are people he does not like he can say the normal consumption is very high and a small duty will be applied on the goods. In other words, any possibility of adjudication on shelf goods, taking all the objections into account, will be prevented by subsection 3 of section 2A as it is now.
I say, why is this government trying to override the courts, trying to prevent people getting into the courts, to have the facts decided? The facts should not be decided in a back room down on Mackenzie avenue, they should be decided openly when they are in dispute and before a proper tribunal set up for the purpose. Anything less than that is arbitrary power. You are taking the power to tax away from parliament and doing the
Customs Tariff
very thing the minister objected to so eloquently in 1955. The year 1955 seems to have been a poor year for the minister in setting precedents. In the year 1955, as the hon. member for Laurier has just said, the present Minister of Finance objected to a minister or the governor in council being given certain powers in the event of an emergency threatening our very existence. However, this government suggests now that the Minister of National Revenue should be given arbitrary powers to govern the whole ambit of Canadian import trade, without appeal to anybody.
If one looks at subsection (b) of section 2A he finds that the minister can decide whether or not goods are custom-made. If he says so, that is fine. There is no appeal to anybody. No more arbitrary power over the economy of a country has ever been requested in any document that I have ever seen placed before parliament than the minister is proposing to put in this legislation. The Minister of National Revenue will be able to decide, without appeal, without regard to the facts if he wishes to be capricious, whether goods are shelf goods or custom made. There will be no appeal. He will be able to decide, in the case of shelf goods, what the normal consumption in Canada is. Once he has decided that, any adjudication on the other points will be an utter and complete farce. It is this legislating of the courts out of existence, denying the people the right of appeal to the courts which is, of the many objectionable features in this legislation, the most objectionable.
I ask the minister why he does not ask us to change the law in a fashion that he thinks is right, but leave it to the courts to interpret the law? This is the proper way, under our constitution, instead of substituting the Minister of National Revenue for the courts and providing no right of appeal. There is no right for anyone else to examine the facts in an independent fashion. This is the most arbitrary interference with our trade which, after all, represents the source of the income of 20 per cent of the people of this country. This provision clearly gives to the Minister of National Revenue the power of life and death over the income of a very large proportion of the Canadian people. Compared with anything that was done by the previous administration, the arbitrary character of this legislation is beyond belief.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Before the minister answers, since he was proceeding to reply to what I said, I wonder whether he would not give consideration to one matter which will take just a moment to bring to his attention. I refer

Customs Tariff
to a statement made by the Prime Minister at Cornwall in 1958, and which is reported as follows:
A textile manufacturing city, has been seriously hit by United States "dumping" of textiles, and Mr. Diefenbaker made it plain this situation would not be permitted to continue. The textile industry has not always been treated fairly in the past, he affirmed in a searching denunciation of the former Liberal government. Its requests for better treatment have much too long been neglected.
Notwithstanding the passage of three years, not only has nothing been done but three of these industries have been closed putting out of work some 2,000 people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has his right to speak in the committee. It was interesting to hear him make this speech under the guise of attempting to be of assistance to me and give me an opportunity to continue. I think it would have been much more to the point if he had said he was exercising his right to speak and to raise the questions which he did. I said I intended to deal with these questions. If he will be patient, I intend to deal with them, and deal with them adequately, just as I intend to deal with the points raised last night by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River.
We heard this afternoon the hon. member for Timmins speaking in the same sense as did the hon. member for Laurier this afternoon and somewhat in the same sense as the hon. member for Assiniboia last night in his typically wild speech. The assertion is made that this legislation is an example of a protectionist policy and that in this respect it exhibits a trend. Those assertions 'have no basis in fact whatever. They have no basis in anything except the fancy, the fiction and the political approach of those who resort to such statements.
What is the record of this government with regard to tariff changes? The record, is this. Three regular budgets have been introduced, namely in 1958, 1959 and 1960, in which tariff changes were made. Where those tariff changes involved items with regard to which there were bindings under GATT we have followed scrupulously and to the letter the provisions of GATT. In every case negotiations have been held and what was presented to the house was presented in accordance with the agreements reached with the countries concerned. There has been loyal adherence at all times to GATT, both with regard to its letter and its spirit.
I think it is not unfair also to recall that the tariff changes that have been made, as to the principal items concerned, have been made invariably on recommendations made by the tariff board. Some amendments have been
made, of course, on items that were not before the tariff board but they were not large matters or important and far-reaching amendments. Some of these references to the tariff board had been made by our predecessors before we came into office. Some of these references have been directed to the tariff board since we came into office.
What about the changes themselves? Here is the record. I do not say this is the only way by which to test the effect of budget policies in this regard but I think it is not unfair to tally up the results of tariff changes made in the aggregate in these three budgets, and here they are. There have been 392 changes. Of those changes, 203 were simply formal changes of a mixed character. There have been 65 increases and 124 reductions. Hence, when the hon. member for Timmins talks about a trend under the present government toward high tariffs I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that he just does not know what he is talking about. He has not taken the trouble to inform himself as to the facts. When his leader last night talked about protectionism, again he was speaking not in accordance with the facts but in violation of the facts.
It is a question of the volumes involved, not the items.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As to the volumes involved, may I say this. The matters involving larger volumes were those that were negotiated under GATT. They were those that were passed upon by the tariff board. Does the hon. member not believe that attention should be paid to the recommendations of tariff board? Does he not think that the countries concerned in the negotiations are perfectly competent to judge whether they are satisfied with the changes made? I therefore say that the facts are all against hon. members opposite in this regard.
Then the hon. member for Laurier surprised me very much indeed this afternoon when he talked about the export restrictions applied by the Japanese government on exports of certain commodities to Canada, including a number of textile products. It was at that point that I sought his leave to ask him a question. That leave he denied me. I wished to ask him whether he was opposed to the imposition by the Japanese government of these restraints on their exports of textiles to Canada. He did not give me the opportunity to ask that question, so he has his choice now. Either he disapproves the effort that has been made in discussions with the representatives of the Japanese government to seek such reasonable restraints against the flooding of the Canadian

market by exports into our market in concentrated form or he can, on the other hand, say that he approves those efforts, in which case I think he must withdraw what he had to say this afternoon or admit that he has changed his mind.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit me to reply?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be delighted to do so.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In so far as Japanese quotas are concerned I say to the minister that in my opinion that was not the way in which to protect the textile industry in this country or in Cornwall. The statement made by the Prime Minister in all the textile areas was quite clear, namely that the situation of dumping would be put an end to and would be stopped. That promise has not been carried out. My answer to the question of the Minister of Finance is this. The method which he adopted is not the one which should have been followed. If there was dumping, the one which should have been followed is the one which the Prime Minister himself said he was going to put into effect and which was never put into effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do I correctly understand the hon. member to say that the proper method by which to protect the textile operations in Cornwall, then, was to apply anti-dumping valuations?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. member tell us what method he says should have been applied?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am telling the minister that the Prime Minister made a statement in Cornwall. That statement was quite clear, namely that he would put an end to this dumping in the city of Cornwall and in other textile areas. I do not know what method he intended to use but he indicated that he would stop it in the same way as he stopped the dumping of agricultural products. That was not done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I ask the hon. member whether he wishes to say what method he, the hon. member for Laurier, would apply-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You are the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -in order to protect-and that was the word he used, namely "protect"-the operations of those textile mills in Cornwall. I am asking him what he says would have been the proper method to apply.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have repeatedly attacked the government because of a lack of policy
Customs Tariff
which they have demonstrated with reference to dumping in the textile industry. I reply to the minister now by saying that he is in office or his government is in office, and that it is his responsibility to do away with that situation, not that of the opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have asked the hon. member a plain straightforward question and he has turned his back on it three times at least and has run right away from it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The minister has the answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I took my seat. I gave the hon. member an opportunity to tell me what he would say was the method by which protection should be extended to the textile mills in Cornwall and he still has not answered the question. He has run away from it as fast as his feet will carry him.
You have run away from the Prime Minister's promise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member talked vaguely about dumping.
It was the Prime Minister who talked vaguely about dumping.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, the Prime Minister did not talk vaguely about dumping. The hon. member for Laurier has now had his opportunity to say what he thought should have been done. He said something should have been done to protect the operations of the textile mills in Cornwall, but he cannot or will not tell us what that method is and he is running away from it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The Prime Minister is running away from it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will tell my hon. friend what has been done, and I will tell him what he and his associates have done to try to prevent the government from doing something salutary in this respect.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Let us hear that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member was one of those who sought to prevent the government obtaining at the hands of parliament in 1958 those measures that were asked for to strengthen the enforcement of the law against dumping.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And which you have never put into effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He and his colleagues fought that legislation up hill and down dale.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We certainly did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member is talking out of both sides of his mouth this afternoon. He is talking as though there

Customs Tariff
were need of more rigorous anti-dumping measures, and yet he is one of those who sought to prevent the government from being given by parliament in 1958 powers that were needed to prevent the kind of dumping that had gone on under the Liberal administration.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me finish my statement. He is going on this afternoon on the same tack, pretending on the one hand that he wishes to see textile production in Cornwall protected-he used that expression -but he will not come out and tell us what he would do.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not say any such thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He has had the
chance. He shows he is against anything in the way of tariff protection-
He did not say that either.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman; I made no such statement, because the textile industry in Cornwall exists no longer. It has been put out of business. The question I rose to ask the hon. minister is this : What effect have these tremendous and terrible anti-dumping regulations had upon the textile industry which existed at the time?
And which has disappeared now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
there are several answers to that. The first one is that the neglect by the former Liberal government to take measures that should have been taken by them had gone so far at that time that it was not possible to save those industries in the time that was available to us.
Then why did the Prime Minister promise to do it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This government has done everything that it could reasonably do under the circumstances.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It has done nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And what we did do was done in the face of unrelenting opposition, interference and delay on the part of the Liberal opposition. They tried to deny us the. powers for which we asked in 1958 to deal with dumping, just as today they are trying to narrow down the powers of the government to deal with dumping.
In relation to the textile industry, we referred this matter1 to the tariff board at once in 1957, and in respect to the recommendations of the tariff board in its report we asked 
parliament to carry out those recommendations. When the very first one of them came before this house, hon. members opposite did everything in their power to prevent a very modest increase in the customs tariff on woollen fabrics being legislated in this house. They did their best to prevent that.
I did not expect the hon. member for Laurier to take this line this afternoon. I can understand the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate taking this line, because he is an unrepentant free trader, but I cannot understand a line like this being taken by the hon. member for Laurier, whose position has been, I have always understood, that of a protectionist when it comes to the textile industry. He laughs now. Apparently I have misunderstood him and he is another of the free traders of the Liberal party and does not mind seeing protection withdrawn from Canadian industries that cannot be competitive unless they are given the modest protection that is given to them. Then we have the position taken by the hon. member for Essex East when it comes to protection for the automobile industry.
So we have all categories over there in the opposition. We have members over there who can talk free trade; we have members over there who can talk high protection. It just depends which record you turn on at any particular moment.
I think I have reviewed the record in this respect that was put before the house last night and today by hon. members opposite in very distorted form- Now, if I may, I wish to conclude this part of my remarks with an observation about the position of this government in relation to trade in general.
I have referred to the way in which we have loyally observed the provisions of GATT under all circumstances. I think it is a matter of satisfaction that, far from there being retaliatory measures-as was suggested by the hon. member for Assiniboia last night in an utterly wild statement

the fact is that Canada's export trade has prospered under the present government. Our total external trade in 1960 was the greatest external trade ever carried on in the history of this country. Our exports were at an alltime high. There, in the facts, is the answer to these baseless assertions by hon. members opposite.
I think those persons in this country who are dependent upon industry for employment, and who in many cases are represented by ladies and gentlemen who are in Ottawa today taking part in the presentation of the case of organized labour for certain measures, will be interested in some of the things that were said last night by the hon. member

lor Assiniboia, things that were said in the house this afternoon by the hon. member for Timmins and things that were said here by the hon. member for Laurier.
They will know perfectly well that it accords with the philosophy of those three gentlemen, and undoubtedly the parties that they represent, to deny this protection to Canadian workmen engaged in these industries. These hon. gentlemen would narrow down the interpretation of the words "of a class or kind made in Canada" and would thereby deprive those industries of a measure of protection that was intended to be extended to them by governments right down to 1950 before the process of erosion set in. Because on that matter depend jobs for Canadians. Hon. members opposite seem to be quite ready to overlook the fact that jobs are involved.
I said there were matters raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River with which I would deal. The hon. member asked last night about the interpretation to be given to three expressions that are to be found in the amendment.
The first of these was the expression "adequate facilities exist in Canada". In regard to that phrase, it is considered that there must be in Canada one or more manufacturers, or a combination thereof, who have the required installed manufacturing or producing equipment, coupled with the technical knowledge, required to make the goods in question.
The next question related to the expression "economic production". On this point I say that as costing data will not always be available when considering the status of custom-made goods in the light of this expression, each case

as I indicated yesterday-will have to be examined on its own merits. Factors such as mark-up realized by the manufacturer, and the laid down cost to the purchaser taking into account the incidence of duty based on the goods being regarded as "made" and proper valuation in accordance with the provisions of the Customs Act, must be taken into consideration.
The third phrase the hon. member asked about was "reasonable period of time". In so far as that phrase is concerned, a definite period may not be set without regard to the actual goods under review and the standard established by good business practice in the field involved. Proposed delivery dates in the instances where they are known may serve as a guide in this respect.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister a question? I was just wondering from what document he was reading. Is it a draft of the regulations that we can follow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am referring to my notes, Mr. Chairman. The word "reasonable" is not a new one to the hon. member. This is a standard of conduct that is being interpreted by tribunals every day with respect to all manner of questions. It is not a new concept by any means at all.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I wish to deal with this subject that has been very tangled and confused by hon. members opposite, in relation to the function of the minister and the function of the tariff board under the proposed amendment.
I draw attention again to the two classes of goods that are contemplated by the amendment; first of all the custom-built according to specifications goods, and second the shelf goods. It is in clause 2, subclause 3, that we have reference to the decision of the minister. The clause reads:
The decision of the minister will be final with respect to the following matters:
(a)	The normal Canadian consumption of the goods described in subsection (2).
Now the goods described in that subsection are shelf goods. So the minister is called on to make a simple determination as to what is the normal Canadian consumption of shelf goods, a matter which is not difficult at all. The clause continues:
(b)	whether goods are custom-made to specifications and whether adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time.
That is the only other point which the minister is clothed with power to decide under the terms of the proposed amendment.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is the more important of the two.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The power which is given to the minister is the power to decide into which of the two classifications the goods in question fall-are they custom-made according to specifications, on the one hand, or are they shelf goods. These are not difficult matters to determine at all. It is not a difficult question involving processes of law or legal determination for a minister to say, on the one hand, these are goods custom-made according to specification or, on the other hand, they are not of that class and are, accordingly, shelf goods.
Would the minister permit a question on that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am right in the middle of an explanation-

Customs Tariff

The minister has referred to subclause 3 where his decision is final with respect to the normal Canadian consumption of goods described in subclause 2. Would the hon. gentleman reconcile that with his statement yesterday, reported at page 1367 of Hansard, when he outlined three items which would still be eligible for appeal. Item (b) was the determination of the amount of Canadian production. Are we not talking of the same thing in this resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the hon. member has misapprehended what is involved here. On the one hand we are dealing with Canadian production. The other concept is that of Canadian consumption, and these are two different things.
I was in the middle of my explanation with respect to clause 3(b). I was pointing out that the other matter which arises for decision by the minister is whether adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time. These are all matters which are capable of decision in the light of statistical analysis. This is the sort of thing which is involved in decisions by government departments day after day. These are not matters of a nature which calls for judicial determination as related to questions of interpretation of words, or questions of law related to the interpretation of words in statutes. Therefore, these are eminently suitable matters for decision by the minister.
Jurisdiction in this form has very great advantages for the business community since it is possible for the minister to make quick decisions, whereas if those decisions were to be left to delay, those whose business it is or those whose interest might lie in delay could delay decisions on these simple questions for very long periods of time. As a matter of fact, through no fault on the part of the government department concerned, delays amounting to years have occurred in such situations. Therefore we are seeking this method of greatly improving the administration in this respect by putting simple decisions in relation to matters which are capable of relatively simple statistical determination into the hands of the minister for prompt decision.
The usual argument for arbitrary power.

Would the minister permit a question? What is the definition which the hon. gentleman conceives under the clause which speaks of goods being custom-made to specifications? The minister did suggest that it referred to heavy machinery. If it is to be restricted to heavy machinery only, why

does not the bill say that it is to be so restricted? Otherwise, the minister or the officials of his department will have to wrestle with a whole range of problems when they have to adjudicate on what is custom-made to specifications and I certainly would not wish to be an official of the department charged with the duty of wrestling with this definition. Perhaps the minister could clarify the position.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. member for Cartier that he will not be faced with the prospect which he fears and that he will not be called upon to make such decisions as an official of the department.
May I say that yesterday afternoon I gave illustrations of the type of goods to which this definition will normally apply. I do not anticipate the slightest difficulty in connection with these words, as to finding what are custom-made goods according to specifications. The hon. member knows what specifications are. He knows when goods are made up on a customer's order according to specifications. It is obvious that this relates to heavy machinery-quite heavy machinery -and the sort of thing, which is based on specifications; engineering specifications, for example.
You say the same words over and over again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hope the hon. member understands them, because they are relatively simple. If he does understand them, then he has grasped the point.
Textiles could be made to specifications.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, that is not the type of goods here-
Then why not say so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The textile goods that I know of would, I think, in all cases be shelf goods. Of course, the words "shelf goods" do not appear here. The hon. member will realize that what I have called shelf goods are the residue-all kinds of goods except those which are custom-made to specifications. Surely the phrase presents no difficulty. We would look for the order- something made up according to specifications. Engineering specifications would be a good example. Heavy machinery used in the manufacture of textile goods might be an example.

May I give an illustration to the minister which might help him clarify the situation a little. It is possible to order textile goods made in another country, requiring that this textile contain so many-

squares to the inch, be of such and such a colour, or quality and so on. Those are specifications for custom-made textiles, according to our normal understanding of the English language. If the minister intends that only hard goods, machinery and equipment, should be covered, then I think the legislation should clearly say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You can have shelf goods made up according to specification, but that does not make them custom-made goods according to specification.
What is the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can anticipate no problem in relation to determination here. I think the line of definition is drawn quite simply by this legislation.
What are custom-made goods, leaving aside the word "specifications"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Goods that are made up specially in response to a particular order.
That is correct. That could be the case with textiles, though.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But this is a combination of the two things you have here. You have custom-made goods and, I stress this, the phrase "according to specifications".
May I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I finish dealing with one question at a time?
You have not dealt with it yet, but carry on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not see how
I can with the hon. member contributing his interruptions.
The hon. member for Cartier talks about custom-built goods on the one hand and specifications on the other. Here there are the two requirements. It is the union of the two.

Will the minister permit me to direct this question to him. If I went to the United States and ordered some shirts to be made of a particular cloth to particular measurements to suit me, would those be custom-made goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Those would not be custom-made goods according to specifications, Mr. Chairman.

With deference, Mr. Chairman, they are custom-made goods, made to specifications; so when are custom-made goods made to specifications not custom-made goods made to specifications?
Customs Tariff
No one can challenge the minister's interpretation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. For the sake of orderly debate I would ask hon. members to put questions but not make a speech.
I asked a question which the minister made no attempt to answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
For the enlightenment of hon. members opposite, here is a declaration made by the tariff board in a
case:
The significance of much of the evidence and argument can be seen most clearly when related to certain facts which are not disputed concerning the building and installation of newsprint machines in Canada. Newsprint machines are not produced for stock. Each machine is made to order in accordance with detailed specifications agreed upon by manufacturer and user; it is seldom a precise duplicate of any other newsprint machine but normally it resembles several of them very closely. The building of a machine normally requires many months. In Canada production and consumption of newsprint machines have been very irregular; in some periods many machines have been installed, in others none.
It will be seen that this is the distinction that has been adopted in the legislation that is now before the committee. We are dealing here with goods-obviously machinery in large part-of a kind that is not sitting in stock. It is not produced for stock. It is made to order in accordance with detailed specifications agreed upon by manufacturer and user.
As would be the case with my shirts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman-
They are not from stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member perhaps wears unique shirts.
The arms are a lot longer than yours.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
With initials embroidered on the pocket?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are other parts of the anatomy than the arms which are of considerable importance in this context.
Some parts of yours are pretty thick.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suppose we are what God made each of us, but we are responsible for what we do with what He gave us, and the hon. member and I will have to leave it at that I suppose.
Passing the buck again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member talks about his shirts-
