He has lost his shirt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would have
thought that shirts would be an article carried in stock as a rule. Shirts can be produced for stock-
So can a machine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think the hon. member is going to say that the shirts he wears are so unique as not to be capable of resemblance to other products of the same kind or that they are never carried in stock or that production is irregular. I would have thought that shirts were a staple commodity notwithstanding the fact that the hon. member, as he said, takes a very long arm.
I have been trying for some time to deal with this subject of tariff board jurisdiction and ministerial jurisdiction. I have dealt with the provisions of subclause 3 in relation to the power of the minister to make decisions and have pointed out the very limited nature of that power.
Let me conclude by reiterating what I said yesterday, that the regular existing appeal procedure to the tariff board remains open to importers with respect to these much more difficult and involved questions: (a) whether or not imported goods are of approximately the same class or kind as goods made in Canada; (b) the determination of the amount of Canadian production; and (c) whether or not the number of articles manufactured in Canada does in fact constitute a minimum of 10 per cent of normal Canadian production.
Normal Canadian consumption.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The suggestion that sweeping, arbitrary powers are supposed to be conferred upon the Minister of National Revenue is totally erroneous. That assertion completely falls to the ground.
Just because the minister says so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Power is conferred upon the minister to make certain decisions with respect to matters that call for decision in the light of statistical data on matters that essentially call for swift decision, the kind that cannot be made in any other quarter than by the minister. Therefore we are presenting to the committee what is a very workable and sound proposal, one that in my respectful submission removes from the governor in council powers that the Liberal government conferred on the governor in council in 1936 and used all the remaining years that it was in office and we instead invite parliament to do the legislating.
The effect of. this legislation so far as the function of the minister and the tariff board 
and the courts are concerned will be to preserve all that is desirable and necessary and helpful in relation to the right of appeal so that there may be no such thing as persons being denied their due rights by arbitrary decision, for the power of the minister to make decisions is confined to a narrow and proper field. This is a very workable scheme and will undoubtedly contribute very greatly to improved administration for the benefit of the business community.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, for the hon. member for Laurier to compare this legislation with the kind of legislation under debate in 1955 when I made certain observations about the arbitrary powers sought by the government of that day at the hands of parliament in relation to the Department of Defence Production is to try to compare day with night. That legislation sought arbitrary power-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We will show the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -that was so sweeping in its terms that the minister of defence production of that day, had he chosen to exercise those powers, could, as I said in that speech, have held the Canadian economy in his hands. He could have changed it. He could have introduced socialism overnight if he had chosen to do so, so sweeping were the powers. To compare those sweeping powers with the limited powers conferred here upon the minister-necessary powers to make decisions essential to the benefit of the business community, prompt decisions-is to compare day with night. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, we present this to the committee as sound, workable legislation without the arbitrary features in it that hon. members opposite think that they see in it but which do not exist in fact.

Mr. Chairman, I must admit I have found the debate this afternoon most confusing. Depending upon who is speaking, the Minister of Finance is either a saint or a sinner. I hope in the course of my questioning to find out if the hon. gentleman is a saint, a sinner or a combination of both.
Of all the important matters that come before this house I have always found and still find the question of tariffs one of the most complex and confusing. Because of that I have no hesitation in saying I do not consider myself an expert with respect to tariff policies. That being the case I shall not be dogmatic in anything I put forward. The reason I rise in my place is that I feel it is necessary for some of this confusion compounded to be cleared away. As one of the representatives of British Columbia in this House of Commons I feel it is my duty to draw the attention of the minister to those

fears which are being expressed in our province relative to the proposals he has placed before us.
I made reference a few moments ago to the possibility of the Minister of Finance being a saint or a sinner. From what I have heard thus far from industry in British Columbia it would be my conclusion that he is a sinner, and therefore it is of the utmost importance in our province, if the primary and the manufacturing industries have misinterpreted what will be the effect of the proposals of the Minister of Finance, to have the matter clarified. In the interests of British Columbia we must know whether there is a mistake in interpretation. If there is a mistake in interpretation, now is the time for the fears of the primary industry and the manufacturers of British Columbia to be cleared away.
This morning I received a lengthy communication from R. H. Ellison, executive vice president of Canadian Collieries Resources Limited. In the past few days I received, as I know the Minister of Finance has also, communications from C. B. Dunham, chairman of the British Columbia loggers association, W. R. Malpass, president of the truck loggers association, and R. T. Rose, general manager of the Vancouver board of trade. These men represent major industries and associations in British Columbia. In all of these letters to me, and in all of the copies of letters or telegrams sent to the Minister of Finance, there is general agreement that they are distinctly worried and fearful of the proposal regarding tariffs being placed before us at this time. I have arrived at a sort of conclusion now. If these big associations and organized industries have reached certain conclusions, then I think we should know from the Minister of Finance whether these conclusions are correct. If not, how did the economy in British Columbia go wrong?
According to the information from the executive vice president of Canadian Collieries Resources Limited, there is a strong feeling that any item which falls into the category of class or kind made in Canada, under the policy being enunciated by the minister, will be in this position. There will be an increase in the price to the consumer or user of between 15 per cent and 20 per cent. That is the reaction they have.
I was also supplied information relating to a statement made by Dr. Purdy, president of the British Columbia Electric Company Limited, to the effect that the turbine which they are to buy from the United Kingdom will increase in cost from $34 million to $39 million under one other proposal.
I get the impression that the fear of these people is that the major impact of this
Customs Tariff
change will result in an increase in the cost of the tools of production. From the letters that I have received from the Vancouver board of trade, the manufacturers association, the loggers association, the Canadian Collieries Resources Limited and the truck loggers association, I have come to the conclusion that they have interpreted the proposal of the minister-I presume they have their economists, statisticians, experts and so on-to mean an increase in the basic cost of the tools of production. This, of course, is a matter of the utmost importance to British Columbia.
As a member of this house I am vitally concerned with the general good of all Canada. However, it is understandable that I am vitally and particularly concerned with the economy of British Columbia. When I hear from my people in British Columbia that this is going to mean a basic increase in the tools of production of the primary and resources industries of British Columbia it becomes a most serious problem. We all know-it has been pointed out by the Minister of Finance and others-that we are already facing difficulties of a competitive nature. I can say this definitely for British Columbia because of the problems we are facing. Anything which increases our cost of production places us in a most invidious and difficult position, in an attempt to produce for a competitive export market.
Not only do I want to express the problem with respect to establishing primary industry in this country, but to say this. If their interpretation and understanding of the problem is correct, then it most certainly is going to discourage to a great extent the possibility of the establishment of new industries in our province and the expansion of those already existing.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, at the dinner recess I was pointing out the fears which have been, and are still being expressed by the primary and manufacturing industries in British Columbia relative to their interpretation of the impact in that province of the proposals that have been set forth by the Minister of Finance. It has been pointed out to me during the dinner hour that this fear is being expressed only in British Columbia. If that is the case, then it is of the utmost importance that every measure be taken by

Customs Tariff
the Minister of Finance in this House of Commons to so explain his proposals that that fear may be alleviated.
However, I have also heard others in this house who do not come from British Columbia express similar fears. In addition, if I gather aright from what was said by the minister this afternoon, particularly in the latter part of his remarks, these proposals are in tune with GATT and in tune with our good neighbour policy with the United States. I do not find that to be the case. I should like to make a brief mention of a publication which is entitled, "Washington through Canadian Eyes". This publication is published privately and is circulated privately to Canadians. I should like to quote from the issue of January 17 of this year, and this is what it says:
While the Canadian removal of tax incentives for American investment in Canada captured all the headlines in United States, it is the customs action on "class or kind" that really has shaken official Washington. Over at the commerce department, officials can become almost livid with anger in discussing this action which they feel endangers much of the U.S., machinery exports to Canada. The state department takes a less anxious view, but remains concerned, nevertheless. At commerce, you even hear talk about retaliation. And one other thing this Ottawa action has done is to provide more ammunition to the protectionists in the U.S. congress.
If the information which was published on January 17 by this publication "Washington through Canadian Eyes" is authoritative at all there is some concern in the United States about the proposed customs action, especially as it relates to the interpretation of class or kind. I quite understand why there might be concern in the United States if this action could interfere with exports. The anxiety which I have been trying to express, as it exists in British Columbia, relates to the possibility of an increase in the cost of the basic production machinery in British Columbia. The vast majority of production machinery is not produced in our province but has to be freighted in and the increase in cost of production machinery, whatever that may be, can be passed on only to the consumer.
As I mentioned previously, we already have enough difficulties in meeting the competition which faces British Columbia as an exporting province at existing prices without having any increase in our cost of production. I do not know whether they are livid in the commerce department in Washington, but I do say that according to the information sent to me, whether or not it is justified, the logging industry in British Columbia is pale with anxiety. If my memory serves me correctly, 54 cents out of every dollar of revenue the people of British Columbia receive comes from

our forest resources. What affects the forest industry is, therefore, of the utmost significance to us. Both the B.C. loggers association and the truck loggers association are deeply concerned. Whether or not they have grounds for this concern, I am raising this matter now so we can hear from the Minister of Finance.
On January 13 of this year the B.C. loggers association informed me through a letter that the introduction by the Minister of Finance in his baby budget of matters having to do with goods of a class or kind not made in Canada is causing grave concern to the manufacturing end of the forest industry in the Pacific province. I can understand that because anything that could result in an additional tariff burden on the forest industry, dependent as we are in British Columbia on foreign markets and faced with competition as we are, is most vital. It was for that reason that on January 13 a telegram was sent to the Minister of Finance over the signature of the chairman of the B.C. loggers association and the president of the truck loggers association. Since a copy of this telegram was sent to me, I hope you will not mind if I read it. It reads as follows:
The logging industry on this coast have noted with much concern that portion of Customs Tariff resolution Hansard page ten seventeen December twentieth. To us it would seem that benefits expected to accrue to one form of industry in Canada could be more than offset by harm to manufacturers of primary products dependent upon foreign markets for their existence. Crippling of the position of mills buying logs from the independent logger can only result in critical harm to his position. On behalf of the loggers represented by our associations we respectfully ask that the suggestion of the manufacturing branch of our industry be enacted as a part of the proposed legislation and that end-use items be provided for all phases of production and manufacture of wood products not now included in the four eleven series.
As this is a concise setting forth of the problem as viewed by those two associations in a telegram directed to the Minister of Finance I sincerely hope, that without my having to go into the matter in more detail on this particular phase, he will give us officially the answer to the anxieties therein expressed and will perhaps go further and make specific comment on the communication which I understand he received under date of January 27 from the Vancouver board of trade.
The Vancouver board of trade is made up of hundreds of the primary and secondary industries of the province of which I happen to have the honour of being one representative. They also express fears similar to those which I outlined to the committee as expressed by the executive vice president of Canadian Collieries Resources Limited and

the logging industry. In this the most recent letter they definitely express a vivid concern about the possible effect on our British Columbia industries primarily involved in export trade. The board of trade, which have research men and statisticians at their command, and the representatives of the major industries of our province in this letter have no hesitation in coming back to the problem, namely that an increase in the price of the production tools in our export industries would make it harder, if not impossible, for them to compete in world markets.
I was most interested in one of their recommendations to the Minister of Finance. I hope the minister will inform us whether he or his departmental officials have made a study of the recommendation of the board of trade for a change in part of the wording of the resolution he is presenting to the committee. As has already been expressed by hon. members who have previously spoken, the board of trade considers that the word "approximately" used in the phrase "goods approximately the same class or kind made in Canada" is capable of too broad an interpretation to be administered equitably. I know that the minister had something to say on this word "approximately" this afternoon but I hope he will enlarge upon what he said previously.
It has been suggested to the minister that in the wording he is recommending to the House of Commons he include some of the words he used in his budget speech. Those words are "goods which are similar in nature and purpose". It is felt by the Vancouver board of trade that these words could, with great advantage, be included.
I may say that I have gone over this matter three or four times and I believe that it reads like a good suggestion. I certainly would be most interested in hearing from the minister whether he can meet the request for the change as set forth by the board of trade. If this request were met, the proposed legislation would then read as follows:
2A. (1) for the purposes of this act, goods shall be deemed to be of a "class or kind" made or produced in Canada if
(a) in the case of goods other than goods custom-made to specifications, goods of the same class or kind, similar in nature and purpose, are made or produced in Canada.
This proposed change seems to meet some of the objections that have been raised in British Columbia.

In essence, the hon.
member would leave out the word "approximately". Is that the idea?
Customs Tariff

Yes; and put in, after the words "same class or kind", the words "similar in nature and purpose". I think the minister would get away from a great deal of difficulty if this suggestion were accepted and I most sincerely commend it to him.
I do not think I need to continue at any greater length, Mr. Chairman. As I stated when I first rose to speak on this subject, to me the question of tariffs has always been a complicated and complex one; indeed it is so complicated, complex and confusing that I honestly admit that I find it difficult on many occasions to understand it. I therefore do not pretend to be an expert. However, as one of the representatives from British Columbia, having received all these communications and telegrams from responsible organizations of industry, both manufacturing and primary, and from such associations as the board of trade, I felt that it was my responsibility to bring the matter forward at this time and to say this to the Prime Minister and to those who maintain that there is no need for such fears or anxieties and that British Columbia apparently is the only province that feels this way. I hope the minister will be able to clarify the situation, and if what he says is correct, then put it in such a manner that there is understanding in British Columbia. If you do not do that, I am afraid that the complex will continue, something that is dangerous for our economy in the battle we now face and shall face in the months ahead, not only to maintain our industry in present production but to extend it in the way which is so necessary for the maintenance of our standard of living and in order to extend prosperity across the nation as well as to maintain it in British Columbia.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps with the permission of the hon. member for Stormont I might deal with this matter that has been raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is a fact that we have had representations from, I believe, seven associations in British Columbia connected with the forest products industry. We have not had representations from similar organizations in other provinces. I think there have been just two other formal representations from the rest of Canada and they were both from importers.
The hon. member, of course, is perfectly justified in raising this question and I am glad to have an opportunity of dealing with
Mr. Chairman, could I ask the minister to comment on the proposed change of the Vancouver board of trade to the definition of "class or kind".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I am glad the hon. member has reminded me of that. Various wordings were considered when the decision was taken to put the legislation forward in this form. On careful consideration it was considered that the word "approximately" was the best word to use under all the circumstances here, rather than such words as were suggested by the board of trade, namely "similar in nature or purpose".
I point out that words like "similar in nature or purpose" would open up an entirely new realm. It should not be thought, I think, by those who put this suggestion

forward that they are putting forward something that would be more restrictive than the word "approximately". As a matter of fact, having regard to the fact that the word "or" is used in this expression "similar in nature or purpose," there is very good reason for thinking that the word "approximately" is more restrictive than would be the words suggested by the board of trade.
After all, goods could be similar in purpose without being similar in nature and this kind of expression would take us, I think, pretty far afield. So I think that while the hon. member considered that the words that were being suggested by the board of trade were more restrictive in their effect than the language proposed in the amendment, I would have to take a contrary view.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks this evening will be brief. I must say that I was extremely touched by the solicitude of the hon. member for Laurier, who spoke before dinner, regarding Canadian Cottons and the constituency of Stormont, more particularly Cornwall. I am especially touched by this solicitude because this industry of Canadian Cottons is one which he and his colleagues had neglected for 22 years, and the constituency of Stormont is one which he himself abandoned. I regret that the hon. member is not in his seat at the moment. I had the pleasure of sharing a very delightful occasion with him a few minutes ago. We were both at a reception by the Montreal Trust, but I regret that he has not yet returned.
I believe that the hon. member for Laurier, my predecessor, is having a death bed repentance in the same way the Liberal party at their recent convention had a deathbed repentance. That is the only explanation of the fact that they promised everything that they neglected to do for the previous 22 years. I think it is also significant that my hon. predecessor ran away from the question of the Minister of Finance. Time and again the Minister of Finance reiterated the question: what would you do? In each case the hon. gentleman evaded giving a direct answer. I think it is very significant that he abandoned committing himself in the same way that he abandoned Cornwall after he had abandoned the Cornwall canal to the Americans.
I would like to confirm what the Minister of Finance has said, namely that Canadian Cottons, which I know very well and where I had so many friends working, because of 22 years of neglect by the hon. member for Laurier and his colleagues, has disappeared, before even the very salutary action taken by this government to reverse the situation could take effect as it has done with regard
Customs Tariff
to so many other textile firms in this country. The former employers, the former workers and the former union men in my constituency will never forget the attitude of my predecessor and, more especially, of his colleague the late Mr. C. D. Howe who was of the opinion that this textile industry was obsolete and expendable. He made that opinion very clear indeed. These people will never forget that, nor will they forget the obstructionism and delaying tactics on the part of the present official opposition-I would hate to call it the effective opposition-to this present constructive measure now being brought in to assist and protect the hard beset manufacturers in this country and, in turn, provide so many more jobs for our people while at the same time not interfering with our obligations under GATT or the export trade of the rest of the country.
In closing, there are a few other things I wish to say. I referred a few minutes ago to abandonment. I understand that many people in Quebec are referring to my predecessor as a refugee from Cornwall. Furthermore, many of his former friends, who know him far better than I know him, have been going so far as to regard him as a renegade. Again, in closing, let me pay a tribute to the people of Stormont who have snatched victory out of defeat. They have made the best of a bad situation. They have taken these cotton mill buildings and formed a limited dividend company, a development company. In these buildings they have almost a million square feet of floor space to rent at advantageous rates in order to attract new industries to this area. There is no greater bargain in this whole country for any new industry than our people have provided in Stormont, and I predict that very shortly this enterprise will bear fruit. Let me say that the imagination and enterprise of these people in Stormont and of my constituents in Cornwall is unprecedented and that it has set an example to all the people of this country. Ever since 1812, as I have reiterated in this house, when our people of Cornwall commenced the construction of the Cornwall canal-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I remind the hon. member that we are discussing a resolution concerning the Customs Tariff. I notice that in his speech the hon. member has made many references which are not relevant.

I was just referring to the commendable way in which my constituents have reacted to the difficulties created by my predecessor and his colleagues because of their customs policy. But, let me say, because of this fallacious, this iniquitous, this unwarranted, doctrinaire, free trade

Customs Tariff
policy which has been such a disaster to this country and which has placed us in our present difficulties; because of this and also because of the loss of the Cornwall canal to which I referred earlier, Cornwall, my home town and my predecessor's town, was stranded high and dry like a gasping whale on a rocky shore left dry by the receding tide of Liberalism, but because of the provision of $400,000 for a new harbour and the great tide of legislation which this government has brought in, once again Cornwall is afloat and once again it will find itself in the position it deserves and enjoying the prosperity to which it has been accustomed.

I should just like a moment in which to reply to the insinuations made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat in the course of the high-minded speech he delivered about the hon. member for Laurier. I think the committee ought to know that the hon. member for Laurier is at a meeting this evening of the University of Ottawa, his alma mater, having to do with the expansion of that institution. That is the only reason my hon. friend is not here tonight.
The hon. member for Laurier had no hesitation about referring to my constituency when I was in conference with members of the Canadian Catholic Federation of Labour this afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I, myself, unfortunately had to be out of the house this afternoon for the same reasons as the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Stormont. I, too, had appointments which prevented my being here, so I did not have the opportunity of hearing all the debate. It may be, therefore, that for a minute or two I shall be dealing with straw which has already been threshed. But having had reports sent me of what has been said during the debate so far, I know there has been some criticism raised of the fact that apparently the Minister of National Revenue, who happens for the moment to be the person standing in front of you, has power to decide this and to decide that. Apparently some hon. members believe that is a most iniquitous position in which any minister could be placed, that it is a regression to the days of R. B. Bennett, and all the other cliches with which hon. members opposite try to appeal to the house sometimes when they are entirely devoid of arguments.
There is nothing new about the fact that the Minister of National Revenue has power to decide this, that and the other. I have not had time to check carefully the Customs Act, but I have gone over it in the last few minutes-
It is the Customs Tariff with which we are dealing; that is the act which is before us.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The Customs Act is also one which I administer. The Customs Tariff is the one which falls in the province of the Minister of Finance. Take, for example, that section of the Customs Act which deals with valuations for duty. It is clearly set out that where the valuation for duty cannot be determined under certain preceding sections-and there are five of them-the value for duty of goods shall be of such value as the minister may determine. Mr. Chairman, believe it or not, this statute was not brought in in 1958 in the amendment to which the hon. gentleman from time to time refers; this amendment was brought in under the benign Liberal leadership of that great patron leader of Canada, Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, and therefore that power must be sacrosanct, the fact that the minister when he brought in legislation could be endowed with such power-
It was not frozen as final.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
It is final. This is final. There is no appeal provided in the sections from which I am reading. I am not reading sections relating to class or kind. I direct the attention of hon. members to subsection 11, under which the minister may reduce the value for duty and so on. I invite hon. members to turn to subsection 12 under which it may be found that the minister may fix the value. I direct the attention of the committee to section 38, subsections 1, 2 and 3 under which there is reference to the same power. If one had time I am sure one could go on and give other examples.
All I am saying is that there has been recognized for years and years in the administration of the Customs Act and in the administration of the Customs Tariff for which I am responsible, that there must be decisions made with fairness, with equity and with some degree of celerity and speed. You cannot hold goods in a warehouse for anywhere from six to nine months when an importer is awaiting delivery of those goods until someone makes up his mind and reference of the matter is made to various officers and so on. In simple, elementary but practical things, the Minister of National Revenue has been endowed with power under previous governments.
I referred to the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King. Frankly that provision may well have been in existence before he became prime minister. It has been on the statute books for a long while. I am simply stating it as a recognized principle. There is nothing

to which one could take exception in the fact that the Minister of National Revenue has the power to do this or that.
To hear some of the discussion this afternoon and yesterday one would think that class or kind legislation was something new, a departure from past practices, an iniquitous conception, something which this Tory government seeks to bring into the house hankering back to the days of R. B. Bennett. Class or kind legislation was in effect when I became minister and has been in effect, indeed, for many years. The history of this legislation has been referred to in this debate. It is well known that it extends back over decades.
Scarcely a week goes by but that the Minister of National Revenue makes rulings with respect to class or kind. I made three last week and indeed I make them all the time. When I say that, I do not mean I make one every hour. Perhaps days or a week will go by without my making one and then perhaps in the period of one day I will make three or four.

Would the minister permit a question? Would he indicate to the committee what change is proposed in this resolution vis-a-vis the previously existing conception, particularly when it involves the Liberal administration, that in so far as class or kind made in Canada is concerned the question of substantial production in Canada has a bearing?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Under the order in council to which reference was made by my colleague when he opened this debate it has always involved 10 per cent production of those goods of a class or kind made in Canada. That has been the provision for many years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For 25 years.
Since 1936.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: My friend the hon. member for Ottawa West says since 1936. It was at that time the order in council was passed.
It did not prevail under the Bennett regime.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
No. My hon. friends opposite love to refer to R. B. Bennett and the terrible things that will happen if this legislation is enacted. Personally I have no fear of returning from time to time to the regime of R. B. Bennett. At least, one could find there some integrity and determination and various qualities which perhaps have not been entirely predominant in the regimes which immediately followed the Bennett regime.
My hon. friends opposite see shadows and ghosts. I believe that you, Mr. Chairman,
Customs Tariff
were in the Chair two years ago when we brought in amendments to the Customs Tariff and were told that we would raise the tariffs as high as Haman's gallows. On that occasion the shadow of R. B. Bennett was walking the floor, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was almost in hysterics thinking about what would happen in respect to it-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is a daily occurrence.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
-but, as we see, the world has gone on very nicely ever since. I refer my hon. friends opposite to a quotation which I vaguely remembered from having attended Sunday school. I checked the scriptures tonight and I think this quotation might be offered as a timely word of advice to hon. gentlemen opposite who never have anything realistic to deal with and therefore always have to deal with imagination and ghosts and things which they fear may happen. Before they go to bed tonight I urge hon. gentlemen opposite to read the thirteenth verse of chapter 18 of Proverbs, according to which they will find that:
He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
I suggest that my hon. friends stop answering these things before they hear them because it is a shame and a folly and it is above all a shameful waste of time to have a debate on such imaginary and dreadful things as they conjure up before us without any foundation in reality whatever.
With respect to class or kind and the rulings made by the minister from time to time, it is true that there is some technical differentiation-or will be if this amendment is approved by the house-in relation to the matter of appeals. Substantially, however, the appeal procedure is exactly the same. I observe that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate shakes his head. I will tell the hon. gentleman how realistically this matter is approached. How many appeals have we had? What is there of which we may be deprived?
What about the right?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Hon. members opposite are not being deprived of anything because the only matter with respect to which the minister can make a determination under the proposed legislation are substantially statistical information which is available to the dominion bureau of statistics in any event and is a matter of commonsense computation and nothing else. In any event, whatever the appeals may have been, I find that going back over the last 10 or 15 years there have been seven appeals made on seven different rulings.

Customs Tariff
That is all the erosion amounts to, then?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: There also have been several appeals made of one ruling and several of another. The hon. member talks about erosion-
It was the Minister of Finance who talked about erosion.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: My hon. friend says that the Minister of Finance spoke about erosion. Another hon. member asks: Why do you bring this in? I did not hear the debate this afternoon or last night.
The minister is not following his own advice now. He is answering without having heard it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I did not hear the remark made by the hon. member for Trinity. I believe he was worried this afternoon about having his shirts made to order. Well, my arm is longer than his, so I am faced with exactly the same problem he is and I buy my shirts in Canada-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: -so the hon. gentleman need not worry about the class or kind ruling.
I buy my shirts in Canada, too.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member does. He would never be elected in Toronto if he did not.
My hon. friends talk about erosion and class or kind rulings. Here is one example the minister gave in respect to a famous case relating to the manufacture of car wheels. One had a spindle which was perpendicular. The wheel went around the perpendicular spindle and the centre was cut out into which the axle went. It was held by the department to be of a class or kind made in Canada. Another was imported and it was a horizontal spindle and the wheel went around in the fashion I now describe with my hands. The tariff board said it was of a class or kind not made in Canada. That is an example of class or kind and of erosion.
Let us take the case of the shovel. We were making power shovels in this country of two cubic yard capacity. The plant was there and they were producing them all the time. They had the machinery, equipment, experience, men and the orders for shovels of a capacity of two cubic yards. Then shovels of a two and a half yard capacity came in from a foreign source. There was an appeal. The tariff board said despite the fact that there were men who were out of a job, despite the fact that there was the plant, equipment and experience, that two and a half yard

shovels were not of a class or kind made in Canada. That is a class or kind ruling. That is an example of erosion. That is the shovel case. If my hon. friend wants the reference I can give it to him.
I have the judgment upstairs.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
It is appeal No. 306. The
decision was given on May 20, 1954. Then, there is the ballbearing case and the .22 rifle case. In one case, if it was fed manually, it was of a class or kind. If there was a little attachment to it, it was not of a class or kind. It was because of decisions such as these that we have introduced the legislation. I could go on, but I am not going to bore the committee by giving the cases. There have been others since 1949, but without questioning the judgment, the whim or whatever the philosophy of the persons who were writing these decisions, the fact remains that from 1949 and 1950 there has been a complete erosion of the principle of class or kind. Surely, Mr. Chairman, when you get a shovel which has a capacity of two yards and another one with a capacity of two and a half yards, both powered in the same way, both manufactured in the same way, both performing in the same way, you cannot say that one is a different class because it happens to have a half yard more capacity. It is not identical and that is why we used the word "approximately" to cover such cases as those I have mentioned.
I could go on, Mr. Chairman. But I think there has been a great deal of misapprehension, which my colleague has cleared up, in talking about this matter, as though this were something revolutionary, something new. It is new in so far as goods made to order are concerned, and for the moment I am not dealing with that. This is a matter which we can discuss later on, as the committee desires. But I am dealing just now with goods of a class or kind which are made in Canada. It is because of this erosion, because of the things which have happened, which I am certain was never the intention of parliament when parliament enacted the statutes, that we have introduced this legislation.
It was never the intention of the various Liberal ministers of finance-and when I say "Liberal" I mean Liberal with a capital "L"- under the Liberal regime and the various ministers of national revenue that this statute would be applied in that way. All we are trying to do is to restore what in our opinion was the intention of parliament when it passed this legislation. We are not going back to the days of R. B. Bennett; we are simply going back to the practices which were pursued, and I think properly so, by the

government of Mr. Mackenzie King, and those associated with him, up until at least 1950.
There are other things I could say about this, but I think we have at least cleared away the background in so far as I am concerned because I have had pretty close experience with this now for almost four years. I could have checked it; I did not have time to do that, but I have given score of rulings. As industry changes, as we move ahead, for instance, in the plastics field today and in the field of drugs-and there are a score of fields -we make class or kind rulings very frequently. I make many a year, and very often several a week.
My friend from Vancouver East was talking about the lumber business and quite properly what this might do to that industry. I think my colleague replied to that effectively and fully. This also might be said. In that industry you are dealing not with machinery made to order, generally speaking, I would think, but with saws and planes and with production machines. Generally speaking, you order this material from a factory.
Oh.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
My hon. friend says "oh". I think that is right. I have had some experience in the lumbering business. Generally speaking, it is a different thing entirely from manufacturing, shall we say, a generator or a turbine generator, which takes two years to build and is built to a new specification. You buy your equipment. It is true there are variations in size and so forth, but generally they are of a class or kind which can be manufactured and supplied within 48 hours, or a week after the order. If there is a class or kind situation there the rulings must have been given before. Many of those machines which are used in that industry undoubtedly have had a class or kind ruling. Therefore, there is going to be no change under this legislation unless, of course, some new machine is developed which has not been envisaged so far, and on which there could be substantial manufacture developed in Canada.
All I am saying, Mr. Chairman, is that we should look at this realistically. This is nothing new. This is no attempt to raise tariffs, or anything of that kind; it is simply, in so far as this phase is concerned, class or kind of goods made in Canada. It is simply an attempt to restore the law to the situation in which it was, and the reason for that is the attrition which has taken place and which has had the effect to quite an extent, shall I say, of weakening the position of Canadian industries.
As I said, when you cannot tell whether when you have a shovel which is two yards and another one which is two and a half yards, that one is of a class or kind and the
Customs Tariff
other is not, you are really working on an even more theoretical position than the fears of my hon. friends opposite in dealing with this situation tonight.
When you come to those goods made to order, I could say something on that because of the experience we have had-
Before the minister goes on with that-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I do not intend to.

-I have one question I should like to ask. Why does the government now consider it is necessary to take away from the tariff board the capacity to decide on an appeal what the normal Canadian consumption of the goods is? That is the question I ask the minister. The minister says no change is being made, but this is a very substantial change. Our argument is that no effective adjudication can be made at all if one of the questions of fact is decided finally by the minister and cannot be considered in the appeal. That is a change in the law, abolishing the right of appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue

The statement is very general, but as a general proposition and allowing for generalities, the answer is yes. But that is not the point. What I want to get at here is the use of the word "erosion" by the Minister of Finance. He bases his whole argument on the fact that the interpretation was eroded. I,	for one, am a bit mystified about the other legislation that is on the order paper having to do with increasing the number of members comprising the tariff board. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have never seen such straddling of the fence as the hon. member is doing now.

I am not straddling the fence. I am expressing my views and I am prepared to defend them. I think the Minister of National Revenue is aware of the problem with which I am trying to deal. It is of real concern to the country in general and, I may suggest, to his area of the country in which I think it is the honest wish of all Canadians that there be more development of industry.
There is this proposition to be considered. When you get certain types of machines for use by manufacturers, on which they are dependent for a product to be manufactured, one particular machine with some slightly different characteristics may do the job at a rapid rate and extremely efficiently whereas another machine, which is remarkably similar but which perhaps does not have the same raise to it or does not have the swing characteristics to it, will not do the job efficiently. In one particular case I have in mind the difference in the duty was 22J per cent. If the ruling in that case was in accordance with the definition in this resolution the result would be that the plant would not have been established. I am happy to say the decision was under the kind of rulings that the minister's colleague described as erosion. It was treated as of a class or kind not made in Canada and the plant is now in extremely successful operation.
I want to go a step further and point out this consideration. Depending on the product being manufactured, the cost of machinery for the manufacturing operation can have a large importance in the final cost of the articles being manufactured. That is where the difficulty lies in this problem. That is why I am concerned with what I regard as an extremely loose definition in this new legislation being offered to the committee and for which the resolution is being submitted now. I am rather concerned about it.
It is all very well for the minister to charge us with having fears of return to interpretations in former days of Prime Minister Bennett and so on. I do not want to rehash that

old ground. Admittedly there was a high tariff movement in those days and legislation was submitted directly for that purpose. I will not re-argue the merits of it now. After reading this legislation and having observed the minister's curious attitude in presenting it-I refer to the Minister of Finance-the only way in which I can assess it and size it up is this. I think it is an attempt to do indirectly the same sort of thing in that connection that was done in that other era directly.
Having said that I admit that there are difficulties in the interpretation of class or kind; I am prepared to admit that there may be some need for clarification in the light of experience over the years because the tariff has in it a great number of items and some sections of it can get into an area where there is a whole new technology and development and so on. So I am not saying there is no need for any legislation on the subject, but I am saying that, looking at this legislation, it is an attempt to do indirectly what the government is not willing to do directly and what it is wrong to do.

Canada" regulations-which are the essence of the statutory revision before us at the moment-that this developed in a very clear way in 1936 when Canada decided to enter into a broader trade agreement with the United States.

Even prior to the opportunity for parliament to rectify some of the offensive restrictions that had developed during the Bennett regime prior to 1936, when we were entering into new faith with the United States on a broader range of trade, there were certain stipulations. One of those stipulations was set out in a letter dated November 15, 1935, on the very day this new trade agreement was signed. It reads as follows:
In Interpreting the words "of a class or kind made or produced in Canada", provision will be made to make it clear that the phrase "made or produced in Canada" in this context means "made or produced in Canada in commercial quantities" and arrangements will be made-*
This was a pledge of our embassy at that time:
__for giving adequate notice of the transfer, for

We know that to a tremendous degree our international trade depends upon working out proper arrangements with the country to the south of us. We know that the Minister of Finance, not only in his budget speech of March last but in his so-called baby budget of December 20 expressed some alarm that in this area there might be some risk of a diminution of our over-all volume of trade. The minister did indicate on December 20 and again yesterday, in his remarks in connection with the Customs Tariff Act... speechtext: No; the statute itself is called the Customs Tariff.

I know that in connection with income tax we say the Income Tax Act and I thought, when we look down and see in paragraph 1 that the said act would be amended, perhaps the word "act" should have appeared earlier in the resolution. However, I do not want to be diverted by what I describe as an incidental point.
The minister took great pains on December 20 and again yesterday to say that in his view at least technically, and from the point of view of language and phraseology, he felt

he could stand as a very honest man in connection with any negotiations in which he was participating as a representative of Canada with respect to our GATT trade relationships. That may be, but before we proceed very far I should like to have some further up-to-date information as to the present status of our all too vital negotiations in connection with GATT which have been taking place since last fall and which, unfortunately, we learned from the well informed financial press are not proceeding very satisfactorily as far as Canada is concerned. In preparation for yesterday's discussion, the minister very carefully prepared, in writing, and then read, certain definitions which I felt were required by the committee in connection with this legislation. "Reasonableness", "economic production" and so on were defined. I do not think the minister today did in similar fashion indicate what was to be his view or the view of his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, when we

come to the word "approximately" which also would seem to be a key word in the resolution which is before us. I should like to draw this question again to the attention of the minister.
I spoke to the minister this afternoon indicating that I felt he had not answered the question I raised yesterday with respect to his assertion that it was obvious and clear that in the past ten years decisions of judicial bodies such as the tariff board, the exchequer court, the supreme court and so on had very patently led to an interpretation which was contrary to what the minister thought was the view of parliament. The Minister of National Revenue to a certain extent dealt with that tonight. I think this is basic to our discussion which involves an apparent need, as far as the ministry sees it, for something new in the definition of what is class or kind, made or not made or produced in Canada.

Naturally we shall say that if a ratification is required the ministry should not be afraid to bring forward that definition or bring it back if we are persuaded it is a bringing back and there was an original intention that has been subject to erosion by judicial decision that should be presented before the committee. Mr. Chairman, if I may deal with the balance of the questions asked by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, first let me comment on the origin of the so-called 10 per cent rule. It was in November of 1935 that a note was sent by Canada to the United States. At the time of the signature of the 1935 Canada-United States trade agreement. That note contained a paragraph under which Canada undertook:
-to make it clear that the phrase "made or produced in Canada" in this context means "made or produced in Canada in commercial quantities".
It was pursuant to that undertaking that the King government in the budget of 1936 introduced what is now subsection 10 of section 6 of the Customs Tariff.
That is the "substantial quantities" item for order in council, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. I referred this afternoon to the order in council of July 2, 1936, P.C.-1618, that was then promulgated

in pursuance of the authority conferred by subsection 10 of section 6. The point to note is that the undertaking which was given to the United States by Canada in that note referred to "commercial quantities". Those are quoted words. This phrase was not defined. The decision to implement by the 10 per cent rule which is now to be found in subsection 10 of section 6 was a decision of the Canadian government of the day and this particular formula was never bound.
Mr. Chairman, would the minister assist me. My notes have gone to Hansard. Was it "commercial quantities" or "substantial quantities"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
"Commercial quantities" were the words used in the note given by Canada to the United States. The expression used in section 6, subsection 10, is "substantial quantities".
Just to complete my comment, Mr. Chairman, I had just finished saying before dealing with that question that the particular formula was never bound. Moreover, I would say that the commitment contained in the note presumably expired when the 1935 trade agreement between Canada and the United States was superseded by later agreements. It was never incorporated in any subsequent agreement.
The next point raised by the hon. member concerned the United States. We have had discussions with representatives of the United States government on this subject. They were naturally curious to know what might be the effect of this legislation. There have been discussions and I think it may be said that the representatives of the United States government are continuing to follow this matter with interest.
I am sure they would.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They have received the explanations that have been given to the committee yesterday and today, explanations that I am quite sure would satisfy any reasonable person.
The next point raised by the hon. member concerned the definition of the word "approximately". This is the key word in subclause (a) of the resolution. The primary purpose of the introduction of this word is to change the concept that goods to be of a class or kind must be virtually identical goods. Recent decisions of the tariff board have pointed to the narrow interpretation placed on the phrase "class or kind" to the point where goods must be practically identical before they may be rated as being of the same class or kind. This, we say, is a rigidity that was never intended. Under the new definition of the phrase it will be possible

to restore and confirm the broad and historic interpretation which had been applied prior to 1948, with the result that similar goods may be placed in the same class or kind group. My colleague the Minister of National Revenue has given some specific illustrations tonight in that regard.
On this matter of the right of appeal; this subject, with great respect, has been quite misapprehended. The suggestion is that there has been some narrowing of the effective right of appeal. I submit there is no effective narrowing of the right of appeal contemplated by this legislation. I pointed out this afternoon the three matters in which power is given to the Minister of National Revenue to make a decision, and those three matters are essentially questions to be resolved in relation to statistical data. They are not questions that involve the exercise of some judicial process in relation to interpretation of words in a statute. I am sure no one knows better than the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River that on an appeal to an appellate tribunal that tribunal will not enter into a rehearing of determinations of fact. The ordinary rule is that there must be something more than an issue over facts involved.
There are lots of situations under the laws, whether of parliament or of provinces, where the appeal is confined to a question in relation to law or jurisdiction or mixed questions. All that the minister is given power to decide finally is in relation to those three matters I enumerated and those, I have said, are questions essentially of a statistical nature. My colleague made it quite clear this afternoon that under the present practice of the tariff board, when they encounter such question what they do is refer to the Department of National Revenue for information.
I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that a bogey has been set up in this debate in regard to the matter of limitation of the rights of appeal. The right of appeal on essential questions has been retained; the right of appeal from decisions made by the department, and then to the tariff board and thence to the exchequer court and the Supreme Court of Canada. This is simply a bogey that there has been some arbitrary power conferred upon the Minister of National Revenue.
Assertions do not make facts.

speechtext:
Well, then, in view of the fact that the hon. member of Bona-vista-Twillingate says there is not a chance I might just say-perhaps it is unnecessary, in view of what my colleague the Minister of National Revenue said earlier-that the case may be amply documented as to the course of decisions to illustrate what I refer to as the process of erosion.
Perhaps I might just touch very briefly on some of these things. My colleague referred briefly to the decision in regard to the .22 calibre rifles. This is a decision which was made in 1950. The department had held that all .22 calibre rifles were of a class or kind made in Canada. The tariff board decided that the .22 calibre class should be divided into subgroups. They held that the autoloading type rifles, which were not made in Canada, were of a different kind from manually loaded rifles which were made in Canada.
Let us go on to 1952. Here is a decision involving fork lift trucks. The department had held that fork lift trucks of sizes within a certain range were of a class or kind made in Canada. The tariff board accepted this establishment of classes by size range. Now, Mr. Chairman, note that this is a case in which the tariff board upheld the decision of the department on the question of a size range. But what happened later, Mr. Chairman, by 1960, in the light of certain intervening decisions that had been made by the board and by the courts in the meantime? Then came an appeal involving truck mounted cranes. The department had held truck mounted cranes of sizes within a certain range to be of a class or kind made in Canada. The tariff board rejected the range class, indicating that individual sizes were to constitute the criterion. Here is a case where a decision of the board in 1952 in regard to range was completely set aside by the decision in 1960 under strictly comparable circumstances because of the change in the course of decisions in the interval. Does anybody in this house say that it is reasonable to think that it was the intention of parliament that we should reject the idea of a range class, and that individual sizes are to constitute the criterion as to whether goods are or are not of a class or kind made in Canada?
Here is a decision in 1953 involving a Snyder car wheel boring machine. Although it was agreed that the imported and the Canadian made machines performed the same operation on railway car wheels, that is to say, the cutting of metal from the hub thereof, the decision of the board was to the effect that the machines were not of the

Customs Tariff
same class or kind as they operated on different mechanical principles. The imported machine operated through the action of a rotating spindle carrying the cutting tool on the hub of the wheel held stationary by a special holding device; whereas the Canadian made machine operated on the vertical lathe principle; that is to say, the tool bar moves vertically and does not rotate, while the wheel to be bored is held on a rotating table during the cutting operation. One might go on-
Has the minister anything there about the paper making machine which the Minister of National Revenue and I had some discussion about?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am just giving the decisions I have here. Here is a decision in 1954 involving the shovel to which my colleague referred this evening. The department ruled that while a two and a half yard shovel was not made in Canada, it was competitive with a two yard shovel which was made in Canada, and that therefore the two and a half yard machine should be considered of the same class as the two yard machine. The tariff board ruled that inasmuch as no two and a half yard sizes were made in Canada at the relevant time, such machines should be held as of a class not made in Canada.
An appeal was taken from that decision of the tariff board to the exchequer court and the decision of the exchequer court is reported in the 1956 Exchequer Court Reports, at page 379. The exchequer court upheld the decision of the tariff board. An appeal was then taken to the Supreme Court of Canada, and the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada is reported in 1958 Supreme Court Reports, at page 652. The supreme court upheld the decision of the exchequer court with Mr, Justice Rand dissenting. It was following that decision, and the protracted litigation that was involved in
it, that a more definite turn was given to the course of decisions and therefore the tariff board from that point on felt constrained by the decision of the supreme court to give that emphasis that I have indicated and was well exemplified in this very narrow distinction between a shovel with a two yard capacity and a shovel with a two and a half yard capacity.
We say-and this is my final word-that this is not in accord with the intention of parliament; it certainly was not in accord with the intention of the government which introduced this legislation over the years.
Progress reported.

NANAIMO ASSEMBLY WHARF, B.C.   SHEET PILING
speechtext:
1.	Did the Department of Public Works issue a directive to the contractor to use steel sheet piling of Canadian manufacture in the construction of the Nanaimo assembly wharf, Nanaimo, British Columbia?
2.	If so, what is the cost comparison between this product of Canadian manufacture and the imported product?
3.	Is it the practice of the Department of Public Works to insist upon the use of materials of Canadian manufacture?
Question
4.	If so, is there any limit to the cost differential over imported products in directing the use of Canadian materials?
Answer by: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of
Public Works):
1.	Yes.
2.	Using Canadian steel sheet piling driven in place, the price was $86,361.54. The tender using West Germany steel sheet piling driven in place was $74,901.60.
3.	Yes.
4.	Yes. Each project is reviewed on its merits. Canadian parts and materials are however used to the full extent to which the same are procurable, consistent with proper economy and the expeditious carrying out of the contract.
